The modern vowel -a- is after the adverb form (Middle High German -bāre, Old High German -bāro), which came to be used in predicative and then also in attributive position. From Middle High German -ede, from Old High German -ida, from Proto-Germanic *-iþō. Compare the equally rare doublet -te (from Low German). Cognate with Dutch -te, English -th.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form verbs, chiefly from other verbs, but also from nouns and adjectives. The resulting verb often has a…
parole.testo: From Middle High German -eln, -elen, from Old High German -alōn, from Proto-Germanic *-lōną (frequentative verbal suffix). Cognate with English -le (etymology 1), West Frisian -elje, Dutch -elen, Low German -eln, Danish -le, Swedish -la, Icelandic -la.

parole.significato: A suffix of verbs in their infinitive form.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -en, a merger of various terminations in Old High German reflecting different conjugational patterns, namely -an, -ōn, -en (-ien), and -nen, from Proto-Germanic *-aną, *-ōną, *-janą, *-āną, and *-naną.

parole.significato: A suffix forming adjectives denoting being made from a certain substance or having a particular property
parole.testo: From Middle High German -en, from Old High German -īn, from Proto-Germanic *-īnaz.

parole.significato: Forms nouns indicating an inhabitant of a place, or a person originating from a place.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -ære, -er, from Old High German -āri, from Proto-Germanic *warjaz.
From Middle High German vach (“-fold”), from Proto-Germanic *faką (“division, interval”).

parole.significato: Placename suffix: Indicating a place of dwelling; home
parole.testo: From Middle High German and Old High German heim, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz. (In northern Germany, from adaptation of Middle Low German and Old Saxon hēm, from the same Germanic source.) See German Heim, English home, -ham for more.

From Middle High German -māle, from Old High German -mālun, from Proto-Germanic *mēlamiz, instrumental case of Proto-Germanic *mēlą (“measure; time”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian -moal, English -meal, Luxembourgish -mol.

parole.significato: suffix to derive masculine nouns, especially for male animals
parole.testo: Extracted from names such as Friedrich (“Frederick”) and Heinrich (“Henry”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king, ruler”), which is cognate with Latin rēx and Sanskrit रा॒ज्य (rājyá, whence raj). For male animals, its earliest occurrence is in Enterich (“drake”), which is a folk-etymological

parole.significato: Verb suffix for the second-person singular.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -est, from older -es through rebracketing in inverted forms like sizzes du → sizzestu → sizzest du (“do you sit”). Further from a merger of various Old High German conjugation suffixes, from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: Forms superlatives of adjectives and adverbs, sometimes triggering umlaut.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -est, from a merger of Old High German -ist and -ōst, from Proto-Germanic *-istaz and *-ōstaz.

parole.significato: Verb suffix for the third-person singular of the present tense.
parole.testo: From Middle High German -et, from a merger of several Old High German conjugational endings, from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: -ty; used to form numerals denoting multiples of ten
parole.testo: From Middle High German -zic, -zec, from Old High German -zug, from Proto-Germanic *tigiwiz, plural of *teguz (“group of ten”). Cognate with Dutch -tig and English -ty.

parole.significato: beginning at that time or location; from
parole.testo: From Middle High German abe, ab, from Old High German ab, from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab.

From Middle High German aber, aver, from Old High German aber, ābar, abur, aver, avur, afur, from Proto-Germanic *aferą (“behind”). Compare Bavarian owa (“but”), Luxembourgish awer (“but”), Saterland Frisian oaber (“but”), Middle Low German āver, German Low German aver (“but”).
ab- + legen. From Middle High German abelegen, from Old High German *abaleggen, from Proto-Germanic *abalagjaną.

parole.significato: to take off (to remove something that is attached to something or on top of it)
parole.testo: From Middle High German abenëmen, from Old High German abanëman, from Proto-Germanic *abanemaną. Equivalent to ab- + nehmen. Cognate with Dutch afnemen.

From Old High German ahsala, ahsla, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis”). Cognate with Old Norse ǫxl (“shoulder”) and ǫxull (“axle”) (whence Danish aksel, Icelandic öxl), English axle. Also cognate with Latin āxilla (“shoulder joint”), Sanskrit अक्ष (ákṣa, “axle”).

From Middle High German ahzehen, from Old High German ahtozehan, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Equivalent to acht + zehn. Compare Dutch achttien, West Frisian achttjin, English eighteen, Danish atten.
From Middle High German ahzec, from Old High German ahtozug, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutēhundą. Equivalent to acht + -zig.

parole.significato: plowman, ploughman (British spelling) (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ackerman, from Old High German ackarman, from Proto-Germanic *akramann-. Equivalent to Acker (“field”) + Mann (“man”). Cognate with English acreman.

parole.significato: name of the stork in fairy tales and fables among the Germanic peoples and Germans; often preceded by Meister
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German odebar, Old High German ōtibero (also ōtifaro), from Proto-Germanic *ōdaborǭ, *ōdaborą. Compare Dutch ooievaar, Low German adebar, West Frisian earrebarre.

From Middle High German after, from Old High German aftero ("rear; behind; below"; compare Old High German aftar (“after”, preposition, adverb)), from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri (“more aft, further behind”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epóteros (“further behind, further away”), comparative form
From Middle High German an, ane, from Old High German ano, from Proto-Germanic *anô (“forefather”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“ancestor”). Cognate with Latin anus.
From Middle High German ane, from Old High German ana (“grandmother”), from Proto-Germanic *anǭ, related to *anô (“ancestor”). Cognate with Swabian Ahna, Latin anus (“old woman, grandma”).

From Middle High German alwære, from Old High German alawāri (“friendly, good-natured”), from a compound of Proto-Germanic *allaz (“all”) + *wēraz (“true; friendly”). The final -n is an original case ending that was added to the stem in German Low German territory (compare schüchtern). Close cognate

parole.significato: Intensifying prefix for superlatives: very; of them all
parole.testo: From aller, the genitive form of alle (“all”), from Middle High German al, from Old High German al, from Proto-Germanic *allaz. Compare English all-, English alder-.
From Middle High German almehlich. By surface analysis, all- + mählich (“slow”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz; related to Old Norse makligr.
From Middle High German alter, from Old High German altar, from Proto-Germanic *aldrą. Cognate with German Low German Oller.

From Middle High German anebōȥ, from Old High German anabōȥ (“anvil”) (see also anabolz (“anvil”), anabelzi (“anvil”), which are cognate to Plautdietsch Aumbolt (“anvil”)). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bautaną.

18th-century alteration of Anbot, from Middle High German anbot, anpot (14th c.). Compare Dutch aanbod, Middle Low German anbot. Deverbal from anbieten (“to offer”). The alteration is due to the general replacement of the noun Bot (from Old High German bot and Proto-Germanic *budą) with prefixed Geb

parole.significato: tackle, fishing rod (angler's tool consisting of hook (Haken), line (Schnur), and rod (Rute))
parole.testo: From Middle High German angel, from Old High German angul, from Proto-Germanic *angulō, *angô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enk- (“something bent, hook”). Compare Dutch angel, hengel, English angle.

From Middle High German anger, from Old High German angar (“grass plot, arable or pasture land”), from Proto-Germanic *angraz. Cognate with Middle Dutch anger, Old Saxon angar, Old Norse angr (“meadow, pasture ground”).
From Middle High German angest, from Old High German angust, from Proto-Germanic *angustiz.
an- + legen. From Proto-Germanic *analagjaną.

From Middle High German antwürte, from Old High German antwurti, from Proto-Germanic *andawurdiją. The gender change from neuter to feminine is due to semantic association with Frage (“question”). See also antworten. Cognate to Dutch antwoord and Afrikaans antwoord.
From Middle High German antwürten, from Old High German antwurten, from Proto-Germanic *andawurdijaną. By surface analysis, Antwort + -en.

parole.significato: to work (to do a specific task by employing physical or mental powers)
parole.testo: From Old High German arbeiten, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”), from which English orphan is also derived. Cognates include Dutch arbeiden, Old Saxon arvedian, Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌱𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (arbaidjan).

From Middle High German arche, byform of more common arke, from Old High German arka, archa, from Proto-Germanic *arkō, from Latin arca. The expected German form is Arke. The ch-form is native in parts of Upper German. It was reinforced in the modern standard language by the Medieval Latin spelling
From Middle High German ātemen, from Old High German ātamōn, derived from Proto-Germanic *ēþmaz. By surface analysis, Atem + -en. Cognate with Dutch ademen.

parole.significato: also, too, as well (in addition to whatever or whoever has previously been listed)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ouch, from Old High German ouh, from Proto-Germanic *auk. Cognate with Dutch ook (“also”), Low German ook (“also”), West Frisian ek (“also, too”), Luxembourgish och (“also”), Swedish och (“and”), Icelandic og (“and”), Danish og (“and”), and archaic English eke (“also”).
A compound consisting of Auer (not used independently in modern Standard German, from Proto-Germanic *ūraz, *ūrô (“aurochs”)) + Rind (“bovine”). See also the etymology at aurochs.

parole.significato: [with dative] on, upon (positioned at the top of)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. This form with a lengthened vowel is originally Upper German. Central German forms were Middle High German uf and (western) up. Compare Dutch op, Low German op, Luxembourgish op, English up.

From Middle High German ūzganc, from Old High German ūzgang (“exit, outgang”), from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz. Equivalent to aus- + Gang, also analyzable as deverbal from ausgehen. Cognate with Dutch uitgang (“exit”), English outgang (“egress, exit”). More at outgang.

parole.significato: to root out, to eradicate, to extirpate, to purge, to remove entirely
parole.testo: From aus- (“out”) + rotten (“to clear woods”), the latter was a more southern variant of roden, from Middle High German roten, roden, from Proto-Germanic *rudōną.
From aus- + statten (“to stand up”). The core verb statten, now outdated in modern German, is from Middle High German staten (“to help do something; to add”).
From Middle High German bache m, from Old High German bahho, from Proto-Germanic *bakô, an extension of *baką (“back”). Cognate with English bacon and back, which see.

From Middle High German balz, also balzer (“courtship, mop of hair, ponytail”), attested from the 14th century onwards. Compare Middle High German balzieren (“to tie one's hair into a ponytail”). Further etymology unknown. Possibly linked to Proto-Germanic *baltijaz.

Originally an adverb, cf. mir ist bange. From Middle High German bange, an enlargement (with the prefix be-) of ange, Old High German ango (“narrowly, anxiously”), an adverb of engi (“narrow”), from Proto-Germanic *anguz.
From Middle High German barte, from Old High German barta from Proto-Germanic *bardǭ.

parole.significato: greatly, totally, immensely; used with erstaunt (“astonished”) or, less often, other words expressing a sudden reaction…
parole.testo: From Middle High German baȥ, from Old High German baȥ, from Proto-Germanic *batiz (“better”, adverb), comparative of *wela (“well”), whence German wohl. Represents the old adverb form of besser, whose adverbial use developed in Middle High German. Attributive use of bass, in turn, is much more recen

From Middle High German bū, bou, from Old High German bū, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *būą (“building, dwelling”). The plural form Bauten is that of the related Low German Bude (“building”), from Middle Low German bûwete. The singular Baute did not catch on in standard German.
From Middle High German būch, from Old High German būh, from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, body”). More at bouk.

parole.significato: inseparable verbal prefix that signifies touching the object
parole.testo: From Middle High German be-, from Old High German bi-, from Proto-Germanic *bi-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi.
From Middle High German becke, from Old High German becko, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz (“baker”). Doublet of Bäcker.

From Middle High German ber, bere n (sometimes f), from Old High German beri n, from Proto-Germanic *bazją n. Cognate with English berry and eventually Dutch bes. Chiefly in Upper German, the final vowel was lost through early apocope after short vowel + single sonorant. The -e was maintained in the

From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German bigin, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaz (“beginning”), a nominal formation from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną (“to begin”). Cognate with German Low German Begünn.
From Middle High German begraben, from Old High German bigraban, from Proto-Germanic *bigrabaną, equivalent to be- + graben.

From Middle High German behagen, related to Old High German gihagin (“cherished”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bihagōną, from *hagō-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱak- (“to be able”), see also Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬐- (sak-, “to agree”). Cognates include Dutch behagen, Old Saxon bihagon and Old English gehagia

From Middle High German bīht, begiht, from Old High German bigiht, bijiht, from bi- + jiht (“statement, confession”), from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz, equivalent to bei- + Gicht. Cognate with Luxembourgish Beicht, Dutch biecht.
From Middle High German beide, bēde, from Old High German beide, bēde, from Proto-Germanic *bai.

From Middle High German bīl, bīhel, from Old High German bīhal (whence also Bavarian Beichl), attested (in the form witubil) since the 8th century, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bīþlą (“axe”), instrumental noun from *bītaną (“to bite”). Compare Dutch bijl. Conflated early on with Proto-Germanic *b

From Middle High German bīspil, bīspel, from Old High German bīspel (“proverb", "example”), equivalent to bī- (“by-”) + spel (“talk”), the latter from Proto-Germanic *spellą (“news, message, tale”). Cognate with Old English bīspel (“proverb", "example”), English byspel (“example”). Unrelated to spie

From Middle High German beize, from Old High German beiza, from Proto-Germanic *baitō. The word originally had a fricative (Beiße, Old High German beiʒa); the form with an affricate under influence of the verb beizen.
From Middle High German bëllen, from Old High German bëllan, from Proto-Germanic *bellaną, cognate with English bellow, Russian блеять (blejatʹ, “baa", "bleat”).

From Middle High German berouben, from Old High German biroubon, from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną; equivalent to be- + rauben. Cognate with Dutch beroven, English bereave, Danish berøve, Norwegian berøve, Swedish beröva.

parole.significato: to discuss (to converse or debate concerning a particular topic)
parole.testo: From Middle High German besprechen, from Old High German besprechan, besprehhan (also bisprechōn, bisprehhōn), from Proto-Germanic *bisprekaną (“to speak about, discuss, blame”), equivalent to be- + sprechen. Cognate with English bespeak, Dutch bespreken, West Frisian besprekke.
From Middle High German bestān, bestēn, from Old High German bistān, from Proto-Germanic *bistandaną, *bistāną. Equivalent to be- + stehen (“to stand, be on one's feet”).

parole.significato: to bend something, to bow something
parole.testo: From Middle High German böugen, from Old High German bougen, from Proto-Germanic *baugijaną. In early modern German, almost fully merged with related biegen, which used to have the strong 2nd and 3rd persons singular du beugst, er beugt (compare similar archaic forms like du fleugst from fliegen). parole.significato: any large, roundish swelling on the body, e.g. a bump on the forehead or a bubo
parole.testo: From Middle High German biule, from Old High German būilla, būlla, būla, bulla, from Proto-Germanic *būlijǭ, *būlǭ. Cognate with Dutch buil, English boil.

parole.significato: hive, beehive (artificial structure for housing honeybees, excluding the swarm and its combs)
parole.testo: From Middle High German biute, from Old High German biuta, from Proto-Germanic *beudaz (“offering table”).

parole.significato: to keep, to preserve (to maintain the condition of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German bewarn, from Old High German biwarōn, from Proto-Germanic *biwarōną. By surface analysis, be- + wahren, see the latter for more. Cognate with English beware.

parole.significato: morsel; mouthful; a bite of food
parole.testo: From Middle High German bizze, from Old High German bizzo, from Proto-Germanic *bitô. See the verb *bītaną (“to bite”). Cognate with Old English bita. In Dutch beet, English bit, this word has been merged with Proto-Germanic *bitiz, whence German Biss. (English bite is a new derivation from the verb
Alteration (after the verb bitten) of obsolete Bete, from Middle High German bete, from Old High German beta, from Proto-Germanic *bedō. Doublet of Bede. Cognate with Dutch bede.

From Middle High German blīben, belīben (“to remain in the same position, pause, blin”), from Old High German bilīban (“to remain”), from Proto-Germanic *bilībaną (“to remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Dutch blijven (“to remain”), English belive (“to remain,

parole.significato: to dazzle; to blind (confuse someone’s sight by means of excessive brightness)
parole.testo: From Middle High German blenden, from Old High German blenten, from Proto-Germanic *blandijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. Cognate with Dutch blenden, Old English blendan.
From Old High German bliuwan, from Proto-Germanic *blewwaną, compare English blow.

From Middle High German blic, from Old High German blik, from Proto-Germanic *blikaz, *blikkaz (“shine, appearance, look; metal”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”). Cognate with Dutch blik (“look, glance”), Danish blik (“look, glance; tin”), Icelandic blik (“gleam, shine”), Old English

parole.significato: very red, deep red, blood red
parole.testo: From Middle High German bluotrōt, from Old High German, from Proto-Germanic *blōþaraudaz (whence also English bloodred). Analysable as Blut (“blood”) + rot (“red”).

From Middle High German blode, from Old High German blōdi, from Proto-Germanic *blauþijaz, *blauþaz (“weak, soft, timid”). Cognate with Old English blēaþ (“gentle, shy, cowardly, timid; slothful, inactive, effeminate”), English blate (“bashful, stupid”) and bloat (“be swollen, be worthless”) and Dan
From Old High German borōn, from Proto-Germanic *burōną.
From Middle High German bōȥeln, iterative of bōȥen (“to hit, strike; to play skittles”), from Old High German bōȥan, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to strike”). Cognate with English beat, which see.
From Middle High German bote, from Old High German boto, from Proto-Germanic *budô (“messenger”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ-.

parole.significato: a roast (big portion of meat, usually cooked in the oven)
parole.testo: From Middle High German brate, from Old High German brāto, from Proto-Germanic *brēdô.

parole.significato: to make dissonant noise; roar, as done by wind or water
parole.testo: From Middle High German brūsen, from Old High German *brūsen, from Proto-Germanic *brausijaną (“to break; crack; crackle”). More at bruise. The sense "to shower" is a back-formation from noun Brause, in turn from the "to make dissonant noise" sense of this verb.

From Old High German brūtlouft, reanalyzed as Braut (“bride”) + Lauf (“run, walk”). This reanalysis is etymologically correct since Old High German -louft is derived from loufan (modern laufen). The formation is of Proto-Germanic origin: compare Old Saxon brūdloht, Middle Dutch bruloft (whence moder
From Middle High German breite, from Old High German breitī, from Proto-Germanic *braidį̄. Analysable as breit + -e. Compare English breadth.
From Old High German brocco, from Proto-Germanic *brukkô, related to *brukiz.
From Middle High German brunft, from Old High German brumft, from Proto-Germanic *brumþiz.
From Middle High German brunst, from Old High German brunst, from Proto-Germanic *brunstiz.
From Middle High German pruot, bruot, from Old High German pruot, bruot, from Proto-Germanic *brōduz (“warmth; brood”).

parole.significato: bridegroom (a man with regard to his wedding)
parole.testo: From Middle High German briutegome, from Old High German brūtigomo, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô. The modern -i- (from Middle High German -e-) is due to palatisation before -g-, which has been pronounced as a fricative in many dialects. The -a- is a northern variant first attested in Middle Low Ge
From Middle High German brüeje, from Proto-Germanic *brōaną, whence brauen. Related to brühen.

parole.significato: to blanch, pour seething water over
parole.testo: From Middle High German brüen, brüejen (“to brew, singe, burn”), from Old High German *bruojan (“to scald, burn”), from Proto-Germanic *brōaną (“to brew”) and related *brewwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrew- (“to boil, seethe”). Compound of Buche + Ecker. The now rare simplex Ecker from Middle High German ackeran, eckern; only once attested in Old High German ekarn. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *akraną, whence also English acorn. An original neuter or masculine whose final -n was interpreted as a plural morpheme and which
From Middle High German buole, puole, from *buolo, *puolo, from Proto-Germanic *bō- (“male relative, kinsman”). Cognate with Middle Low German bōle, Dutch boel. More at bully.
From Middle High German buosem, from Old High German buosum, from Proto-Germanic *bōsmaz. Cognate with Dutch boezem, English bosom.
From Middle High German butze, related to Low German butt (“clumsy”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *buttaz.

From Middle High German bæhen, from Old High German bāen, from Proto-Germanic *bēaną (“to warm”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₁- (“to heat up; bathe”). See also Bad, from the same Proto-Germanic root. (Unrelated to backen.)

From Middle High German tamm. Probably via Old High German *tamm from Proto-West Germanic *damm, from Proto-Germanic *dammaz, though it is sometimes considered a later back-formation from the verb dämmen. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dam).

From Middle High German dampf, tampf, from Old High German thamph, damph, tamph, from Proto-Germanic *dampaz. Given the predominant d- in Old High German and quite frequent attestations with th- in related words, the underlying form in High German is probably *þampaz; also attested in the Old Saxon
From Middle High German danc, from Old High German danc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz. Compare Dutch dank, English thank, Danish tak. More at thank.

From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Silesian East Central German doas, Dutch dat, English that. Doublet of dass. Distinction from dass is purely orthographical convention.

From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Dutch dat, Low German dat, datt, English that. Doublet of das. Distinction from das is purely orthographical convention.

From Middle High German telle, from Old High German *tella, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *daljō. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German delle). The form Tell(e) persists dialectally. Cognate with Dutch (dialectal) del and English dell.

parole.significato: nominative masculine singular definite article, the
parole.testo: From Middle High German dër, from Old High German dër, replacing the original masculine and feminine nominative forms from Proto-Germanic *sa, by analogy with the adjective inflection. Compare also Old Dutch thie and Old English sē where the same process occurred. Cognate with Yiddish דער (der).

parole.significato: the thigh of a farm animal, especially a pig
parole.testo: Formally from dick (“thick”) + Bein (“bone, leg”). Probably an alteration by popular etymology of *Diechbein, from obsolete Diech (“thigh”) + Bein. The former from Middle High German diech, from Old High German dioh, from Proto-Germanic *þeuhą.
From Middle High German diech, from Old High German dioh, from Proto-Germanic *þeuhą. Cognate with Dutch dij, English thigh.

From Middle High German dille, from Old High German dilla, from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ. More at thill. The sense “hallway” is from Middle Low German dēle and its German Low German descendants. The form, Diele, likewise seems influenced by Low German (although it could stem from an attested Middle Hig
From Middle High German dienen, from Old High German dionōn, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōną.
From Middle High German dienst, dienest, from Old High German dionest, dionōst, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz. Compare the Old English þēonest, þēnest. See also German dienen.

Inherited from Middle High German diser/dirre, disiu, diz, from Old High German dësēr, disiu, diz, from the Old High German demonstrative pronoun dër, from Proto-Germanic *sa, from Proto-Indo-European *tód. Akin to Old Saxon these.

parole.significato: wick (porous cord that draws up liquid fuel for burning)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tāht, from Old High German tāht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtu-/*þæhta- (“thread”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to weave”). Cognate with Old Norse þáttr, for which reason the onset t- is an irregular hardening (compare tausend). The modern form is not inherited fro

Compound of Dorn (“thorn”) + Busch (“bush”). Cognate with Dutch doornbos, English thornbush and Swedish törnbuske, all meaning the same and having the same elements (stemming from Proto-Germanic *þurnaz + *buskaz), thus they either share a common Germanic root or are calques of this German term.

Akin to the verb dringen (“to press”). From Proto-Germanic *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”). Cognate with English throng and Dutch drang.
From Middle High German drīzic, from Old High German drīzzug, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz. Equivalent to drei + -zig.

From Middle High German dreizehen, from Old High German drīzehan, akin to Old Saxon thriutein. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þritehun. Equivalent to drei + zehn. Compare Dutch dertien, West Frisian trettjin, English thirteen, Danish tretten.
From Middle High German dreschen, from Old High German dreskan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną. Compare Low German dörschen, Dutch dorsen, English thresh, Danish tærske.

From Middle High German dulten, dulden, from Old High German dulten, thulten, derived from thult, githult (compare modern Geduld), a verbal abstract of tholēn from Proto-Germanic *þulāną (“to bear, to endure”). The denominal verb forms are originally south-western and spread northward during the Mid

From Middle High German tunkel, from Old High German tunkal, tuncal (“dark”), from Proto-Germanic *dunkalaz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʷ- (“to smoke, fume”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dunker, also dunkel). Cognate to Dutch donker (“dar

From Middle High German dunst, tunst, from Old High German tunst, from Proto-Germanic *dunstą (“haze, mist, dust, evaporation”). Related to English dust. The onset d- is already predominant in Middle High German, thus due to irregular re-voicing. The expected form tunst disappears in early modern Ge
From Middle High German durch, from Old High German duruh, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw. Cognate with English through, thorough, Dutch door, West Frisian troch, Yiddish דורך (durkh).
From Middle High German dempfen, Old High German dempfen, from Proto-Germanic *dampijaną (“to dampen, make damp”).

Inherited from Middle High German Tene, from Old High German *Teni, from Proto-Germanic *daniz. The modern D- is Central and Low German (Middle Low German Dēne), reinforced by Danish dansk, Danmark. These latter probably also caused the ä-spelling.

parole.significato: dowel (pin to hold two pieces together)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tübel, from Old High German tubil, from Proto-Germanic *dubilaz, probably derived from *dubjaną (whence English to dub). The modern onset d- is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German dövel and see the obsolete variant above). Cognate with Dutch deuvel, perhaps also

From Middle High German ebene, from Old High German ebanī, noun form of eban (“even”) from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz. By surface analysis, eben (“even”) + -e. The sense “plane” is a semantic loan from Latin planum, whereas the sense “storey, floor” is one from English level.

The now rare simplex Ecker from Middle High German ackeran, eckern; only once attested in Old High German ekarn. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *akraną, whence also English acorn. An original neuter or masculine whose final -n was interpreted as a plural morpheme and which was subsequently made into

From Middle High German ephöu, from Old High German ebhouwi, derived through popular association with houwi (“hay”) from older ebah. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *ibahs, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)ebʰ-. The spelling and pronunciation in modern German used to be Epheu [ˈeːpˌhɔʏ̯]. The contemporary

parole.significato: made of ore, thus of metal, especially iron
parole.testo: From Middle High German ēren, ērīn, from Old High German ērīn, derived from ēr (“ore”), from Proto-Germanic *aiz. Not related with Erz (“ore”), but associated with it.
From Middle High German ēren, from Old High German ēren, from Proto-Germanic *aizāną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to respect”).
From Middle High German eichīn, from Old High German eihhīn, from Proto-Germanic *aikīnaz, equivalent to Eiche + -en.
From Middle High German eigen, from Old High German eigan, from the neuter of Proto-Germanic *aiganaz.

parole.significato: to suit, to be apt for
parole.testo: From Middle High German eigenen, Old High German eiganen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aiginōną. Compare English own, Swedish ägna. Related to eigen.

parole.significato: generally indicating (concrete or abstract/metaphorical) motion into something
parole.testo: Middle High German īn-, a variation (like ein (“indicating motion into something”) as in waldein) of the preposition in, from Old High German in, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. Compare English in-.

parole.significato: entrance (doorway or passageway into a building or other enclosed space)
parole.testo: From earlier Ingang, from Middle High German ingang, from Old High German ingang (“entrance”), from Proto-Germanic *inngangaz. Cognate with Dutch ingang (“entrance”), English ingang (“entrance”). More at ingang.

parole.significato: to invite (to ask someone to come)
parole.testo: From Middle High German īnladen, from Old High German inladōn, inladēn, from in- + ladōn, ladēn (“to invite”), from Proto-Germanic *laþōną (“to invite”). The originally weak verb -laden in einladen and vorladen is unrelated to laden (“to load”), but was early on conflated with the latter.

parole.significato: one (numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 1; first positive number in the set of natural numbers)
parole.testo: Contraction of eines (nominative/accusative neuter of ein), from Middle High German einez, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ainatō, form of *ainaz (“one”).

parole.significato: only used in (sich) eins sein (“to agree”) and (sich) eins werden (“to arrive at an agreement”)
parole.testo: Contraction of eines (genitive neuter of ein), from Middle High German eines, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ainas, form of *ainaz (“one”). Doublet of einst (“once”). That this use is an original genitive results from the Middle High German spelling as well as from the fact that those dialects with

From Middle High German īseren, īserīn, from Old High German īsarnīn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarnīnaz. Equivalent to Eiser (“iron”), older variant of Eisen + -en. Now reanalysable as Eisen (“iron”) + -ern, but historically eisern is itself one of the words that contributed to the development of this
From Middle High German eiteric, eitric, eiterec, eitrec, from Old High German eitarīg, eittarīg, from Proto-Germanic *aitrīgaz, equivalent to Eiter + -ig. Cognate with English attery, Dutch etterig.

From Middle High German eilf, eilef, einlif, from Old High German einlif, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Until the 19th century usually written eilf; the monophthongal form is of Central and Low German origin (Middle Low German elf). Compare Dutch elf, West Frisian alv
From Middle High German einlift, einleft, eilft, from Old High German einlifto, from Proto-Germanic *ainaliftô. Equivalent to elf + -te.
From Middle High German elenboge, from Old High German elinbogo, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô; by surface analysis, Elle + Bogen.
The first element ultimately from Proto-Germanic *alizō, compounded with Beere. Compare Erle.

From Middle High German eltern, from Old High German eltirōn, from Proto-Germanic *alþizô. Compare Dutch ouders, English elders. The form is equivalent to a nominalised comparative of alt (“old”). The according spelling Ältern was common in Early Modern German, but later went out of fashion. Several
From Middle High German enphāhen, from Old High German intvāhan, from Proto-Germanic *andfanhaną. Doublet of empfangen.

parole.significato: to receive (e.g. a present, a guest)
parole.testo: From Middle High German enphāhen, from Old High German intvāhan, from Proto-Germanic *andfanhaną. Equivalent to emp- + fangen and further ent- + fangen. Cognate with Dutch ontvangen, Old Saxon antfāhan.
From Middle High German endelos, from Old High German endilōs, from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz. Structurally Ende (“end”) + -los (“-less”)

parole.significato: a white, dirt-dwelling grub of beetles in the superfamily Scarabaeoidea, for example the European cockchafers, the summ…
parole.testo: From Middle High German engerlinc, from Old High German engiring (10th c.), diminutive of angar ‘large larva’ (compare modern dialectal Anger, Inger), from Proto-Germanic *angaraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engʷʰ-(o)r- (“little snake; eel”) (compare Lithuanian ungurỹs (“eel”), Proto-Slavic *ǫgořь

From Middle High German enikel, enenkel, eninkel, from Old High German *eninkil (attested only in diminutive Old High German eniklīn), from Proto-Germanic *aninkilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“ancestor”).

parole.significato: to see a woman through childbirth; to deliver
parole.testo: From Middle High German entbinden, enbinden, from Old High German intbintan, from Proto-Germanic *andabindaną. Cognate with English unbind, Dutch ontbinden.
From Middle High German entwenen, from Old High German intwennen, from Proto-Germanic *wanjaną (“to accustom”).
From Middle High German ërnst, from Old High German ërnust, from Proto-West Germanic *ernust, from Proto-Germanic *ernustuz, whence also English earnest.

From Middle High German erne f (alongside arn m), from Old High German arn f, from Proto-Germanic *azaniz f. Cognate with Middle Dutch arn, Middle Low German erne, arne, Old English *ern (in rugern). The modern form with an alveolar plosive (first attested in Middle High German ernde f) stems from m

From Middle High German ernen, arnen, from Old High German arnōn, from Proto-Germanic *azanōną. This verb is denominal from the noun *azaniz (“harvest”), which underwent umlaut in inflected forms and was later merged with a related noun to yield modern German Ernte. The verb was continuously adapted

parole.significato: Refers to a neuter noun (person, animal, thing or abstract)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ëȥ, from Old High German iȥ, from Proto-Germanic *it (“it”). Compare English it, which instead descends from Proto-Germanic *hit (“it”). Cognate with Yiddish עס (es).
From Middle High German esse, from Old High German essa (“furnace”), from Proto-Germanic *asjǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- (“to dry, burn, glow; hearth, ashes”). Related to Asche, English ash.

parole.significato: several, a bunch, a number, a good deal
parole.testo: From Middle High German ëtelich, Old High German ëtalīh. The first element is of obscure origin, but possibly related to Proto-Germanic *ehþau (“otherwise, or, but if”), source of modern oder (“or”). The second element is hwelīh (“which, each”). Compare etwas.
From Middle High German eter (“fence”), from Old High German etar (“fence, border”), from Proto-Germanic *edaraz (“fence, enclosure”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *edh-.

From Middle High German etewaʒ, from Old High German eddeshwaz, from edde- + hwaz. The first element is of obscure origin, but possibly related to Proto-Germanic *ehþau (“otherwise, or, but if”), source of modern oder (“or”). Compare Icelandic eitthvað, Dutch ietwat.
From Middle High German iuter, ūter m or n, from Old High German ūtar, ūtir, ūtiro m, from Proto-Germanic *ūdarą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥.
From Middle High German ēwic, Old High German ēwig, from Old High German ewa (from Proto-Germanic *aiwaz, equivalent to German Ehe) + -ig. Compare Dutch eeuwig.

From Middle High German vāhen (third person singular indicative present vāhet, also væhet, indicative past vienc [stem vieng-], also vie (in rhyme), past participle gevangen), from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną.

From Middle High German val (inflected valwe), from Old High German falo, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz. While the variant falb is from the Middle High German inflected stem, the form fahl is based on the uninflected stem. However, the lengthened vowel points to influence by varieties that reduce -lw-

parole.significato: to search (conduct an investigative search operation, usually for persons or stolen/illegal goods)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vanden, from Old High German fantōn, from Proto-Germanic *fandōną (“to find out”), from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass, bridge”). The lengthening of the vowel is irregular; compare ahnden.

parole.significato: A lepidopteran; an insect of the order Lepidoptera (i.e., a butterfly or moth)
parole.testo: Haplology of dialectal German Feifalter, from Middle High German vīvalter, from Old High German fīfaltra, from Proto-Germanic *fifaldǭ, *fīfildǭ (“butterfly”), from Proto-Indo-European *peypel-. Cognate with Dutch vijfwouter, Icelandic fiðrildi, and outside Germanic Latin papilio. Folk-etymologicall

From Middle High German varm, from Old High German farm (“a fast boat, skiff”), from Proto-Germanic *farmaz (“ferry, ship's lading, cargo, arrival”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go across, traverse”). Cognate with Old English farm (“cargo, freight”), Old Norse farmr (“load, lading”), Dutch v

parole.significato: a young and sexually mature bull or cow
parole.testo: From Middle High German vasel (“breeding animal”), from Old High German fasal (“offspring”), from Proto-Germanic *fas(u)laz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *pes- (“penis”).

parole.significato: to hiss, to spit, to growl
parole.testo: From Middle High German pfūchen, phūchen, from Old High German *pfūhhan (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Germanic *pukaną (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). The modern onset f- instead of pf- is from East Central German. Compare English puke.
From Middle High German feim, veim, from Old High German feim, from Proto-Germanic *faimaz. Compare English foam.
From Middle High German vëlge, from Old High German fëlga, from Proto-Germanic *felgō. Cognate with Dutch velg, English felly, felloe.

From Middle High German verge, verje (alongside ver, vere), from Old High German fergo, ferio (alongside fero, ferro), from Proto-Germanic *farjô, agent noun of *farjaną. Related with Fähre, which see for more. The word had been widely obsolete by 1700, but was later revived in poetic language. It h
From Middle High German vërren, from Old High German fërrana, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ferrai, same as English far.
Old High German fersana, from Proto-Germanic *fersnō (“heel”).

From Middle High German vert, from Old High German [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *ferudi, from Proto-Indo-European *peruti. Cognates include Old Norse fjǫrð (“last year”), Sanskrit परुत् (parut, “last year”), Persian پار (pâr, “last year”), Ancient Greek πέρυσι (pérusi, “last year”), Lithuanian perna

From Middle High German veȥȥel, Old High German feȥȥil (“band for fastening and holding the sword”), from Proto-Germanic *fatilaz, from the root of *fatōną (“to hold, seize”). Cognate with Old Norse fetill (“band, bandage, sword-belt”), Old English fetel (“sword-belt”).

From Middle High German vestunge, from vesten (“to fasten, to secure”), from Old High German festen, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz (“firm, secure”). Compare Dutch vesting, English fastness (“fortress”).
From Middle High German virne, from Old High German firni, from Proto-Germanic *fernaz.
From Middle High German vist, from Proto-Germanic *fistiz, from Proto-Indo-European *pesd-. Cognate with Dutch veest and Ancient Greek πέζις (pézis, “puffball”).
From Middle High German vlahs, from Old High German flahs, from Proto-Germanic *flahsą (“flax”).

parole.significato: to plait; to braid; to weave
parole.testo: From Middle High German vlëhten, from Old High German flëhtan, from Proto-Germanic *flehtaną.
From Middle High German fliege, vliege, from Old High German flioga, from Proto-Germanic *fleugǭ. Cognate with Old English flēoġe (>English fly).

Middle High German flettern, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *flutrōną, frequentative of *flutōną (“to float”). Probably related to Low German fluttern. Cognate with English flutter and related to English float.
From Middle High German vlozze, from Old High German flozza, from Proto-Germanic *flutô. More at float.
From Middle High German vluc, from Old High German flug, from Proto-Germanic *flugiz.

From Middle High German vluor, from Old High German fluor, from Proto-Germanic *flōraz. The word chiefly meant “arable land” in High German (see etymology 2). The modern sense was influenced or reinforced by Middle Low German vlōr. Cognate with Dutch vloer, English floor (from Old English flōr).
From Proto-Germanic *flōdijaną.

From Middle High German vleche, from Old High German flah, from Proto-Germanic *flakaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥keh (“flat surface”), found in the second element of English cromlech. Analysable as flach + -e (“ness”).

With irregular stress shift (as in Holunder, lebendig, etc.) from Middle High German forhel, alteration of older forhen, from Old High German forhana, from Proto-Germanic *furhnō, from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“speckled”).

From Middle High German fotze, votze, futze, probably from Proto-Germanic *fuþiz (“vagina”). Duden instead derives it from the same source of faul (“foul, something stinky”). parole.significato: the food of an animal, especially its prey
parole.testo: From Middle High German vrāȥ, from Old High German frāȥ, from Proto-Germanic *fr(a)ētaz, derived from *fr(a)etaną, whence German fressen (“to eat”). Cognate with Dutch vraat.

parole.significato: a journey undertaken to find a future wife
parole.testo: From Middle High German vrīete, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *frijōną.

From Middle High German vröude, from Old High German frewida, from Proto-Germanic *frawiþō (“joy”), derived from *frawaz (“joyous”), from Proto-Indo-European *prew- (“to jump; hop”). Cognate with Dutch vreugde, Low German Freid, Danish fryd, Swedish fröjd.

Inherited from Middle High German vriuntlich, vrūntlich, friuntlich, from Old High German friuntlīh, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndlīkaz, equivalent to Freund + -lich. Cognate with Dutch vriendelijk, English friendly.
From Middle High German vrist, from Old High German frist, from Proto-Germanic *fristiz. Cognate with English frist, first. More at frist.
From Middle High German vrō, from Old High German frō, frao, from Proto-Germanic *frawaz (“quick, glad”). Compare Dutch vrolijk, whence also English frolic.
From Middle High German vrōnlīcham, from Old High German vrōn (genitive singular of vrō (“lord”), from Proto-Germanic *frawjô) + līhhamo (“body”) (from *līkahamô).

parole.significato: merry; cheerful; either as a character trait or fleetingly
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz. By surface analysis, froh + -lich. Cognate to Low German froihlik (frauh + -lik) (Paderbornisch).

From Middle High German vorht, vorhte, from Old High German forhta, forahta, from Proto-Germanic *furhtō (“fear”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥k- (“to fear”). The modern vowel -u- is due to influence by the related verb fürchten. Cognate with obsolete Dutch vrucht (still in godsvrucht), Middle Low
From Middle High German vuoter, from Old High German fuotar (“fodder”). Compare Dutch voer, voeder, English fodder, Danish foder.
From Middle High German vuoter, from Old High German fuotar (“sheath”).

From northern Middle High German ver(e) (13th c.), from Old High German *fera, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ (“ferry”), derived from *farjaną (“to bring, carry”), the causative of *faraną (“to travel”), whence German fahren. From Middle High German fūle, vūle, fiule, viule, from Old High German fūlī, from Proto-Germanic *fūlį̄, derivative of *fūlaz. Equivalent to faul + -e.
From Old High German fimfto, from Proto-Germanic *fimftô. Equivalent to fünf + -te. Cognate with English fifth, Dutch vijfde, Old Saxon fīfto.

From Middle High German vünfzehen, from Old High German fimfzehan, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun. Equivalent to fünf + zehn. Compare Dutch vijftien, West Frisian fyftjin, English fifteen, Danish femten, Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌼𐍆𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌿𐌽 (fimftaihun).
From Middle High German vünfzic, from Old High German fimfzug, from Proto-Germanic *fimf tigiwiz. Equivalent to fünf + -zig.

From Middle High German vüetern, from Old High German fuotiren, derived from fuotar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder”). Equivalent to Futter + -n. Compare Dutch voeren (“to feed”), dialectal English to fodder.

parole.significato: to line (to cover the inner surface of a garment or bag)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vüetern, derived from vueter, from Old High German fuotar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath, wrapping, lining”). Equivalent to Futter + -n. Compare Dutch voeren (“to line”). Probably remotely related to etymology 1, but not identical.

From Middle High German gaffen (“to gape; to stare”), from Old High German *gaffōn, from Proto-Germanic *gapōną (“to gaze, observe”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁y- (“to gape, be wide open”); influenced by and partly merged with Middle High German kaffen, a variant of kapfen (“to look, look surpr
From Middle High German gagel, from Old High German gagel, from Proto-Germanic *gagulaz.
From Gagel and Strauch, from Middle High German gagel, from Old High German gagel, from Proto-Germanic *gagulaz.
From Middle High German gaume, from Old High German goumo, from Proto-Germanic *gaumô, alternative form of *gōmô (whence Old High German guomo).
From Middle High German geburt, gepurt, from Old High German giburt, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gaburdiz, *gaburþiz, *burþiz. Cognate with Old English ġebyrd.

parole.significato: gesture (communicative, interpretable motion of the body)
parole.testo: From Middle High German gebærde, from Old High German gibārida, gibāridī (“demeanor, behavior, character”), from Proto-Germanic *gabērijaną, *gabarjaną (“to conduct oneself, behave”); see the related *gaberaną (“to bear, beget”) for more. Cognate with dialectal German Bärde, German Low German Gebarr

From Middle High German gedult, from Old High German gidult, githult (8th century), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *þuldi. Related to Dutch geduld, Vilamovian gydułd, English thild and thole. See dulden for more.
Old past participle of Middle High German (sich) dinsen (“to expand”, literally “to drag”), from Proto-Germanic *þinsaną (“to stretch”).

parole.significato: the whole of an organism's intestines, guts, insides
parole.testo: From Middle High German gederme, from Old High German gidermi, from Proto-Germanic *gaþarmiją, collective of *þarmaz, whence German Darm.
From Middle High German gevāre, gevære, from Old High German fāra, from Proto-Germanic *fērō. Cognate with English fear and Dutch gevaar.
From Middle High German gefidere, gevidere, gevider, extended forms of Middle High German fider, vider, *fidere, from Old High German fedari, *fidari, from Proto-Germanic *fiþriją.
gegen in compounds. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gagin. Cognate with English gain-.

From Middle High German gehaben, from Old High German gihabēn (akin to Old Saxon gihebbian, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (gahaban), Old English gehabban), from Proto-Germanic *gahabjaną. Cognate with Low German gehebben.
From Middle High German geheiȥe n, variant of geheiȥ m, from Old High German giheiȥ m, from Proto-Germanic *gahait-, deverbal from *haitaną, whence modern heißen (in the sense of “to command”).

From Middle High German gehürnet, from Old High German *gihurnit, from Proto-Germanic *hurnidaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *hurnijaną (“to horn”), equivalent to ge + Horn + -t. From Middle High German gelāz, from Old High German gilāz, from Proto-Germanic *galētą, *lētą (“a letting”). Cognate with Old English ġelǣt, ġelǣte. More at English leat.

parole.significato: a sitting, a clutch or nest of eggs
parole.testo: From Middle High German gelēge, gelæge (“a lying, things lying about”), from Old High German *gilāgi, from Proto-Germanic *(ga)lēgiją, ablaut derivation from *ligjaną, whence liegen (“to lie”). Cognate with unprefixed Old Norse lægi. The form with ⟨e⟩ continues the older Central German spelling, rei
From Middle High German geleiten, from Old High German gileitan, gileiten, from Proto-Germanic *galaidijaną, equivalent to ge- + leiten. Compare with English belead.

From Middle High German gelenke (“joint, bend, waist”), from Old High German gilenki, gihlenki (“abdomen”), from Proto-Germanic *gahlankiją, from *hlankaz (“flexible, lank, slender”). Related to Middle High German lanke (“hip, flank, loin”), from Old High German hlanka (“side, flank, hip, loin”). Co

parole.significato: to emit a loud, clear and strident sound
parole.testo: From Middle High German gëllen, from Old High German gëllan, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną (“to yell”). Cognate with English yell, Dutch gillen.

From Middle High German gelehter, a collective form of Middle High German lahter, from Old High German lahtar, hlahtar (8th century), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”). Cognate with Old English hleahtor (whence English laughter) and Danish latter.

From Middle High German gemeinde, from Old High German gemeinida, probably from Proto-Germanic (though the exact formations vary among and within the later languages), from *gamainiz (“shared, communal”) or *gamainijaną (“to share”) + *-iþō; specifically as gemein (“common”) + -de. From Middle High German gemüese, a derivative of Old High German muos (“food, victuals, porridge”), from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“porridge, food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“wet, fat, dripping”). From Middle High German genoue, genouwe, geneuwe (“narrow, close, exact”), from ge- + nou(we) (“narrow, close, exact”), from Old High German *hnouw (“narrow, close”), from Proto-Germanic *hnawwaz. From Middle High German genësen, from Old High German ginësan, from Proto-Germanic *ganesaną, from *nesaną.

From Middle High German gereht, from Old High German gireht, from Proto-Germanic *garehtaz, from *ga- + *rehtaz. Compare Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (garaihts), Old English geriht, Dutch gerecht. Doublet of korrekt.

From Middle High German giruochen, from Old High German giruohhen, ruohhen, from Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną (“to take care”).

From Middle High German geriusche, from Middle High German rūschen, riuschen, from (unattested) Old High German *rūskōn, from Proto-Germanic *rūskōną (“to make noise”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hrews-, *HrewH- (“to move, drive, agitate”); equivalent to ge- + rausch(en) (“to rustle”).

From Middle High German geschicht(e) (“event, struggle, story, history”), from Old High German gisciht, from the verb Proto-Germanic *skehaną, whence German geschehen. Unrelated to Schicht. Cognate with Bavarian Gschicht and Vilamovian gyśicht.

From Middle High German geslechte, from Old High German gislahti, a collective formation from slahta, from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, related to *slahaną (“to strike, hit”). From Middle High German geswulst, from Old High German giswulst, from the root of Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”).
From Middle High German geselle, from Old High German gisello, gisellio, from Proto-Germanic *gasaljô.

parole.significato: hands, farmhands, (domestic) servants, domestics, the menial staff
parole.testo: From Middle High German gesinde, from Old High German gasindi, gisindi, gisindo, from Proto-Germanic *gasinþiją, from the root *senþ-, sinþ- "to go, travel; seek, aim", from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”). From Middle High German gespan (“clasp; frame, welt”), from Old High German gespan (“clasp; chain, bracelet”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *spannaną. Equivalent to ge- (collective prefix) + spannen (“to span, yoke”). Cognate with Middle Dutch gespan (“clasp; pair; troup”), whence modern Dutch gespan,

parole.significato: conversation, chat, talk (conversing between people or parties, either for pleasure or for business)
parole.testo: From Middle High German gespræche, gesprēche, from Old High German gisprāchi, from Proto-Germanic *gasprakją. Cognates with Low German Gespreek, Hunsrik Gesprech, Luxembourgish Gespréich, Dutch gesprek, Old English gesprecan.
From Middle High German gestade, gestat, from Old High German stad, stado, from Proto-Germanic *staþaz. Cognate with English stathe and Bavarian Gstättn (see also Gstätten).

From Middle High German gesæȥe, geseȥȥe, gesetze, gesōȥe, from Old High German gisāȥi (“seat, residence, camp, backside”), from "where one sits on"; compare German sitzen. Possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic *sētiją. Compare also English seat, Icelandic sæti, Middle Dutch gesaete.
From Middle High German gewin, from Old High German giwin, from Proto-Germanic *gawinną. See gewinnen (“to win”).
From Middle High German gewon, from Old High German giwon, from Proto-Germanic *gawunaz. Cognate with Dutch gewoon.

From Middle High German gewonet (“customary”), past participle of gewonen, from Old High German giwonēn (“to get accustomed, bide, abide”). This verb has been displaced by reflexive sich gewöhnen, from related Middle High German gewenen (“to accustom, make accustomed”). Modern German gewohnt absorbe
From Middle High German gewelbe, from Old High German giwelbi, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbiją (“arch; vault; ceiling”). Cognate with Old English hwealf (“arched or vaulted covering”).
From Middle High German giht, from Old High German jiht, *giht, from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz.

From Middle High German gibel, from Old High German gibil, from Proto-Germanic *gabla- (“top of a pitched roof”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰobʰ-lo-, likely derived from the stem *ǵʰebʰ-l-. Compare Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌻𐌰 (gibla), Old Norse gafl.

parole.significato: to be like, to equal to, to resemble
parole.testo: From Middle High German gelīchen, from Old High German gilīhhon, from Proto-Germanic *galīkōną.

The contemporary form is shortened from Geleise, from Middle High German geleis (“track”), cognate with Middle High German leise, from Old High German leisa, from Proto-Germanic *laisǭ (“track, trail”), from Proto-Indo-European *leys-eh₂-, from *leys- (“to trace, track”).
From Middle High German glīȥen, from Old High German glīȥan, from Proto-Germanic *glītaną.

From Middle High German glit, gelit, from Old High German gilid, collective (with ge-) derivation from lid, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz. Cognate with Dutch lid, gelid, dialectal English lith. Also related with English limb.
From Middle High German glimmen, from Proto-Germanic *glimmaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to gleam, shimmer, glow”). See also Norwegian glim, dialectal Old Swedish glim, glimma.
From Middle High German klucke, derived from the verb klucken (“to cluck”), from Proto-Germanic *klukkwōną, of onomatopoeic origin. The g- by dissimilation.

parole.significato: great heat from (or as if from) something that glows
parole.testo: From Middle High German gluot, from Old High German gluot, from Proto-Germanic *glōdiz. Cognates include English gleed, Dutch gloed, Icelandic glóð, Swedish glöd.
From Middle High German glenzen, from Old High German glanzen, from Proto-Germanic [Term?].
Attested 16th century, but probably older. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz, though similar forms exist independently in many languages. Ultimately onomatopoeic.

Common since the 18th century. Alteration (after Gold (“gold”)) of older gulden, gülden, from Middle High German guldīn, güldīn, from Old High German guldīn, from Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz. Equivalent to Gold + -en. Cognate with Dutch gulden, gouden, English golden.

From Middle High German gram (“displeasure, anger”), from Old High German *gramo, from Proto-Germanic *gramô (“anger”). Cognate with English grame. Akin also to Old Norse gramr (“wroth”) (whence the name of the sword), French and English chagrin.
From Middle High German gram, from Old High German gram, from Proto-Germanic *gramaz.
From Middle High German grane, gran, from Old High German grana, from Proto-Germanic *granō (“awn; bristle; beard hair; moustache”). Doublet of Grenze.
Inherited from Middle High German grāt, from Old High German grāt, according to Pokorny, probably related to Proto-Germanic *granō (“awn”). Doublet of Gräte.
From Middle High German grim (“rage”), from the adjective grim, from Old High German grim, from Proto-Germanic *grimmaz (“fierce, grim”).

From Middle High German grollen (“to debase; lower; humiliate”), from Old High German *grollen, from Proto-Germanic *gruljaną (“to yell; shout at”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to grumble”). Compare English growl.

parole.significato: pit, excavation (man- or animal-made hole in the ground)
parole.testo: From Middle High German gruobe, from Old High German gruoba, from Proto-Germanic *grōbō (“groove, furrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ-, whence also German graben (“to dig”). Cognate with Dutch groeve, English groove, Galician groba. Doublet of Groove.
From Middle High German grœze, from Old High German grōzī, from Proto-Germanic *grautį̄. Analysable as groß + -e.

From Middle High German jesen, from Old High German jesan, from Proto-Germanic *jesaną. Variants with dissimilative hardening j- → g- before front vowels occur since Middle High German. From Middle High German hagel, from Old High German hagal, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz.

From Central Middle High German hager. The word is not originally present in Upper German. The standard literature is inconsistent on whether it was restricted to Central German or if it is also old in Low German (compare late Middle Low German hager). Further origin unknown. From Middle High German halde, from Old High German halda, from hald, from a formation related to Proto-Germanic *halþaz (“sloping, inclined”) (from the slanted nature of large heaps). Other theories derive the word from Proto-West Germanic *hulli (“hill”).

From Middle High German hulfter (“saddlecloth; quiver”) alongside hulft, hulst, from Old High German hulft, hulst (“saddlecloth”, also hulfter, but in a copy from the 14th c.). parole.significato: Indicating that something is generally known, or cannot be changed, or the like; often untranslatable; so, just, simply…
parole.testo: From Middle High German halt, pertaining to Old High German halto (“soon, fast”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *haldiz (related to *halþaz (“inclined”)), an adverbial comparative like *batiz.

From Middle High German hantvol, hantfol, from Old High German hantfol, from Proto-Germanic *handufulliz, *handufullō, equivalent to Hand + voll. Cognate with Dutch handvol, English handful, Icelandic handfylli.

parole.significato: labour, especially of a manual type
parole.testo: From Middle High German hantwerc, from Old High German hantwerc, hantwerch, from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to Hand + Werk. More at handiwork.
From Middle High German harm, from Old High German harm, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz (“harm; shame; pain”).
From Middle High German haȥȥen, from Old High German haȥȥōn, from Proto-Germanic *hatāną.

From a merger of Middle High German hūfe (hūf), houf (houfe), from Old High German hūfo (more southern) and houf (more northern), from Proto-Germanic *hūpô and its ablaut variant *haupaz, respectively. parole.significato: to dwell, to reside (under poor or makeshift conditions, or alternatively evoking the image of a creature in its den)
parole.testo: From Middle High German hūsen, from Old High German hūsōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūsōną. Cognate with Dutch huizen, Low German husen, English house, Faroese húsa.
From Middle High German hechele, from Proto-Germanic *hakulǭ. Cognate with English hackle, Dutch hekel.

From Middle High German hechet, from Old High German hehhit, from Proto-Germanic *hakiþaz or *hakidaz, ultimately from the root of Haken (“hook”) (English hook). Cognate with Middle Dutch heket, Old Saxon hakth, *hakith, Old English hacod.
From Middle High German heiligen, from Old High German heilagōn, from Proto-Germanic *hailagōną. Cognate with Dutch heiligen, English hallow.

From Middle High German heiser (“rough, hoarse”), Old High German heisi (“hoarse”), from Proto-Germanic *haisaz. Cognate with Middle Dutch heersch, Old English hās, Dutch hees (“hoarse”), English hoarse, Old Norse háss.

From Middle High German hel (“resounding, loud, shining, bright”), from Old High German hel (“resounding”), from Proto-Germanic *halliz (“resounding”), from Proto-Germanic *hellaną (“to resound, make a sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, make noise”). Cognate with Dutch hel.
From Middle High German hëllen, from Old High German hëllan, from Proto-Germanic *hellaną (“to resound”).
From the compounding of the prefix herab (“downwards”), from the compounding of her and fliegen (“to fly”), from Old High German fliogan (“to fly”), from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”).

parole.significato: Hessian (native or inhabitant of the state of Hesse, Germany) (usually male)
parole.testo: From Middle High German Hesse, from Old High German Hesso, possibly ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *hatjaną (“to persecute; hate”). Compare Chatti, Chasuarii, Chattuarii.

From Middle High German hinder, from Old High German hintar, from Proto-Germanic *hinder. From Middle High German hirse, from Old High German hirso, from Proto-Germanic *hirsijô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“to feed”).
From the compounding of hoch (“up”) and fliegen (“to fly”), from Old High German fliogan (“to fly”), from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”).
From Old High German hodo, from Proto-Germanic *huþô.

From Middle High German hōn, from Old High German hōna, from Proto-Germanic *haunō, related with Proto-West Germanic *haunijan, << Proto-Germanic *haunijaną (“to shame; embarrass; humiliate”), whence English hean; see there.
From Middle High German hort, from Old High German hort, from Proto-Germanic *huzdą. Cognate with English hoard.

From Old High German huof, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Cognate with Dutch hoef, West Frisian hoef, English hoof, Danish hov, and Swedish hov. Non-Germanic cognates include Russian копы́то (kopýto) and Sanskrit शफ (śapháḥ).

From Middle High German hundert, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”). The Duden derives Middle High German hundert from Old Saxon hunderod.
From Proto-Germanic *hungragaz, *hungrugaz (“hungry”). By surface analysis, Hunger + -ig. Compare Dutch hongerig, English hungry.

From Middle High German huore, from Old High German huora, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”). Cognate with Dutch hoer, English whore, Danish hore, Swedish hora.
From Middle High German huoren, from Old High German huorōn, from Proto-Germanic *hōrōną.
Probably from Middle High German hurrā, an imperative from hurren (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Germanic *hurzaną (“to rush”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).
From Middle High German huosten, from Old High German huostōn from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną. Cognate with Dutch hoesten, English whoost, Swedish hosta.

From Middle High German houfen, hūfen, from Old High German hūfōn, from hūfo (“a heap”), from Proto-Germanic *haupaz, whence English heap.

From early modern German Hüfte (“hips”), plural of Huft (“hip”), itself with paragogic -t from Middle High German huf, from Old High German huf, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeu̯bh₂-. Cognate with Dutch heup, English hip, Danish hofte.

parole.significato: pod, hull, case (also with the particular meanings of botany and ammunition)
parole.testo: Middle High German hülse, from Old High German hulsa, *hulisa, from Proto-Germanic *hulisō, cognate with Proto-Germanic *huljaną and Proto-Germanic *helaną which yield hüllen (“to wrap”) and hehlen (“to hide”) resp. Related with English hull.

parole.significato: hut, cabin, shack, cottage (small house, typically built of light materials rather than stone)
parole.testo: From Middle High German hütte, from Old High German hutta (“hut, cottage”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ, though the word is originally exclusively High German. Further origin unknown. Some theories link it to Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewt- (“to deck; cover; covering; skin”). All related words
From Old High German ira, from Proto-Germanic *hezōi.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *en. More at in and inne-.

parole.significato: only used in inne sein, innehalten, innewerden etc.; inside
parole.testo: From Middle High German inne, from Old High German inne, from Proto-Germanic *innai. Compare Old English inne.
From Middle High German and Old High German irdīn (also erdīn), from Proto-Germanic *irþīnaz (“earthen”). Equivalent to Erde + -en.
From Middle High German irgent, iergen (“somewhere”), from Old High German io wergin, hwergin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hwargin.

parole.significato: obviously; certainly; of course; as you know; as is generally known (indicates and emphasises that one is expressing an…
parole.testo: From Middle High German ja, from Old High German ja, jā (“yes”), from Proto-Germanic *ja (“yes”). Cognate with Yiddish יאָ (yo).

From the respective dialectal words for yes in about half of Northern and Central Germany and all of Western Germany (compare Low German ja, jo). From Middle High German jeten, from Old High German jetan, from Proto-Germanic *jedaną.
From Middle High German jungelinc, from Old High German jungiling, jungaling, jungeling, from Proto-Germanic *jungilingaz.

parole.significato: heifer (young cow that has not calved)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kalbe, from Old High German kalba, from Proto-Germanic *kalbǭ. Cognate with Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌻𐌱𐍉 (kalbō). Related with German Kalb (“calf”).

parole.significato: jug, pitcher, pot, can (container for pouring fluids, especially beverages, often having spout and handle)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kanne, Old High German channa, from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ. Cognate with Old Norse kanna, Old English canne, English can, French canette (“small can”), Gothic *𐌺𐌰𐌽𐌽𐍉 (*kannō).
From Middle High German kar, from Old High German char (“bowl; dish”), from Proto-Germanic *kazą (“vessel; container”).

From Middle High German kūme, from Old High German kūmo, from Proto-Germanic *kūmaz, *kūmijaz (“weak, pitiful, frail”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, cry”). Cognate with English comely and archaic Dutch kuim (“barely”).

From Middle High German kegel, from Old High German chegil, kegil (“peg”), especially pegs for a tent (zeltchegil) or similar. From Middle High German keren, kern, from Old High German kerian, kerien, from Proto-Germanic *karjaną.

parole.significato: to turn (change the direction of movement)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kēren, from Old High German kēren, from Proto-Germanic *kaizwijaną. See char. Cognate with Hunsrik keere.

From Middle High German kīmen, from kīm, kīme (“sprout”) (see Keim). Supplanted or merged with Middle High German kīnen (“to sprout”), from Old High German kīnan, from Proto-Germanic *kīnaną (“to germinate; sprout”).
From Middle High German kërne, kërn, from Old High German kërno, from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”).

From a conflation of Middle High German kuchen (“to breathe”) (from Proto-Germanic *kuh-) and kīchen (“to breathe hard; pant; gasp; wheeze”), ultimately of imitative origin. Compare Dutch kuchen, English cough.

From Middle High German kipfe (“roll of bread”), perhaps related to Old High German kipfa (“axle”), from Proto-Germanic *kippaz (“beam, log”), itself possibly borrowed from or related to the source of Latin cippus (“post, stake”).

From northwestern Middle High German kirn, *kirne, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ. Cognate with Dutch karn, English churn. parole.testo: From Middle High German kirre (“docile”), unrounding of kürre, from Old High German *quirri, *querri, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz (“calm”). Cognate with Danish kvær, Swedish kvar, Gothic 𐌵𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍂𐌿𐍃 (qairrus). The semantic development from “docile” to “confused” may have occurred in the context of flir

parole.significato: fawn (a baby deer, goat, chamois or ibex)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kiz, kitze, from Old High German kizzī, kizzīn, from Proto-Germanic *kittīną (“goatling, kid”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ- (“kid, goatling, little goat”). Cognate with Low German kitte, English chit. Related also to English kid, Danish kid, Swedish kid.

From Middle High German klammern, klammeren, from Old High German *klammarōn, from Proto-Germanic *klammarōną, from Proto-Indo-European *glem-, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to amass, ball up”). Related to Middle High German klemberen (“to stick together, cling”).
Upper German, from Middle High German klimpfen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *klampō, related to Proto-West Germanic *klammjan. Cognate with English clamp.

From Middle High German klāwe, from Old High German klāwa, from Proto-Germanic *klēwō. Immediately cognate with Luxembourgish Klo, Westphalian Low German Klao(we), West Frisian klei, and possibly Dutch klauw. Also related with English claw (from Proto-Germanic *klawō) and Danish klo (from *klōwō).

From earlier kläuen, from Middle High German kleuen, klæwen, from Old High German klawēn, chlawēn, klawjan, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną. From Middle High German kleit, from Old High German *kleid, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt-. Cognate with Dutch kleed, Low German Kleid, English cloth. Possibly related to klettern, Klette, Klei.
From Middle High German kleiden, from Old High German [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *klaiþōną (“to clothe”). Cognate to English clothe.
From Middle High German kleidunge, from kleiden (“to clothe”), from Kleid, from Old High German *kleid, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“cloth”). Cognate with Dutch kleding, English clothing.

From Middle High German klette, from Old High German kletta f, kletto m, from Proto-Germanic *klīþô, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt- (“to cling to, cleave, stick”), from *gley- (“to stick, smear”). Middle High German kluppe, from Old High German klubba. Related to Proto-Germanic *kleubaną (“split, cleave”). Compare Bavarian Kluppn.

From Middle High German knouf, from Old High German knouf, from Proto-Germanic *knaupaz, one of several kn- words related to *knuttô (“knot”). Cognate with Dutch knoop. Also related with German Knopf, Dutch knop and further with German Knubbel, Dutch knobbel, English knob.

From Middle High German knolle, Old High German *chnollo, from Proto-Germanic *knudan-, *knudla-, *knulla- (“lump”), possibly related to Old English cnotta. Cognate with Old English cnoll, Dutch knol, English knoll.
From Middle High German knopf, from Old High German knopf, from Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”). Cognate with Hunsrik Knopp, Luxembourgish Knapp, Dutch knoop.

From Middle High German knüllen, from Old High German knullen, from Proto-Germanic *knuzlijaną (“to bump, to knock, to mash”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *gen- (“to squeeze, to pinch”). Cognate with English knell and Swedish knulla (“to fuck, to have sex”).

From Middle High German kobe (“shed, sty”) (modern Koben) + *holt (“goblin”), from hold (“friendly, gracious”), a euphemistic way of referring to the mischievous beings, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“inclined, favorable”). Related to Dutch kabouter. Typologically compare with English the good folk.

parole.significato: to taste, try (sample the flavor of something)
parole.testo: From Old High German kostōn, from Proto-Germanic *kustōną. More at costen.

From Middle High German krage (“neck”), from Proto-Germanic *kragô (“throat”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ-. Cognate with Hunsrik Kraa, Dutch kraag, probably also English craw; see the English for more (DWDS).

parole.significato: to scratch (rub a surface with a sharp, pointy rough object, especially to remove itching)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kratzen, from Old High German krazzōn, chrazzōn, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gred- (“to scrape”); compare Albanian gërresë (“rasp, scraper”).

parole.significato: to fondle, tickle by scratching softly or running one’s fingertips over
parole.testo: Iterative of now unused krauen, from Middle High German krouwen, from Old High German krouwōn, krouwen, from Proto-Germanic *krawwōną. Compare Dutch krauwen. From Middle High German krūs (“frizzy”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), of unknown origin; possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of hair”). parole.significato: loop, curl, squiggle (something roundish, especially a loop of writing or of something spiral-shaped)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kringel, diminutive of krinc, from Old High German *kring, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz, whence Dutch kring. Chiefly a Central German, i.e. northern, word, reinforced by Middle Low German kringel.

parole.significato: crop, craw (part of a bird's throat)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kropf, from Old High German kropf, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz. Cognate with English crop, which see.

parole.significato: basket, pannier, especially one borne on the back
parole.testo: From Middle High German kretze, from Old High German krezzo, from Proto-Germanic *kradô ~ *krattijô. Cognate with Dutch krat, English crate. Compare with roughly synonymous Kraxe (older also Krächse). Both words very probably influenced each other.

parole.significato: pie; cake; tart (foodstuff made of baked dough, other than bread)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kuoche, from Old High German kuohho, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô. Compare Dutch koek. Doublet of Quiche.
From Middle High German kumpf, kumph (also kump, komp), from Old High German *kumpf, *kump, *kumb, from Proto-Germanic *kumbaz.

From Middle High German and Old High German kunst (“knowledge”), first attested in c. 9th century; related to the verb können. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunstiz (“knowledge, ability”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). Cognate with Dutch kunst, West Frisian keunst, Swedish konst.
From Middle High German kutel, from Old High German kwedilla, from Proto-Germanic *kweþuz (“stomach, belly”).
From Middle High German kemmen, kemben, from Old High German kemben, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną (“to comb”).
From Middle High German quërder, from Old High German quërdar, from Proto-Germanic *kwerþraz (“bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷérh₃-tro-s, from the root *gʷerh₃- (“to devour”).

From Middle High German küelen, from Old High German kuolōn, chuolen, from Proto-Germanic *kōlōną, *kōlēną, related to *kalaną (“to be cold”). Equivalent to kühl + -en. Cognate with Hunsrik kiele, Luxembourgish killen, Dutch koelen, Saterland Frisian köile, English cool (verb), Swedish kyla.
From Middle High German küene, from Old High German kuoni, from Proto-Germanic *kōniz. Cognate with Dutch koen, English keen.
From Middle High German lache, from Old High German lacha, lahha (“swamp, marsh”), from Proto-Germanic *lakō (“lake, pool”). See variant Lache for more.

parole.significato: spawn (eggs laid in the water by aquatic organisms)
parole.testo: From Middle High German leich. Identical with Leich and thus ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laikaz (dance, game).

From Middle High German laster, from Old High German lastar, from Proto-Germanic *lahstrą (with regular loss of h before st), a variant form of *lahtrą (whence Old English leahtor and Dutch lachter), from the root of *lahaną (“to blame, fault, reproach”) (whence also Old Norse lǫstr and its descenda

parole.significato: foliage, greenery, leaves (on a tree or fallen onto the ground, but particularly the latter)
parole.testo: From Old High German loup, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“peel, break off”). Compare Low German Loov, Dutch loof, English leaf, Danish løv.
From Middle High German louf, from Old High German hlouf; louf, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupą.
From Middle High German lëdic, lëdec, from Old High German *lidig, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.

parole.significato: feud or fief (estate granted to a vassal by a feudal lord)
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *laihną.

parole.significato: woe, grief, distress, sorrow, suffering, affliction
parole.testo: From Middle High German leit, from Old High German leid, from Proto-Germanic *laiþą, related to *laiþaz (“loath”). Cognate with Dutch leed, English loath. Originally unrelated with the verb leiden (“to suffer”), though the two stems early on began to influence each other. See leid for more.

parole.significato: line, cord (a rope, usually relatively thin), especially
parole.testo: From Middle High German līne, from Old High German līna, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“rope, string”).

parole.significato: last (tool for shaping or preserving the shape of shoes)
parole.testo: From Middle High German leist (“foot trace, last”), from Old High German leist (“foot trace, last”), from Proto-Germanic *laistaz. Cognate with Dutch leest, English last, Swedish läst.
