From Middle High German leiter(e), from Old High German (h)leitara, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidrijō.
From Middle High German lende, lente, from Old High German lentī, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄.

From Middle High German lette, from Old High German letto, from Proto-Germanic *ladjō-, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂t- (“moist, wet”). Cognate with Icelandic leðja (“mud, muck”), Welsh llaid (“mire”), Lithuanian latakas (“gutter”), and possibly Latin latex.

parole.significato: to injure, to harm, to hurt, to punish etc.
parole.testo: From Middle High German letzen, from Old High German lezzen, from Proto-Germanic *latjaną.

parole.significato: reputation; reports about someone; opinions about someone
parole.testo: From Middle High German liumunt, from Old High German hliumunt, from Proto-Germanic *hleumundaz (“reputation”). Cognate with Sanskrit श्रोमत (śromata, “fame, renown, glory, celebrity”). parole.significato: a person (often, but not necessarily, female)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *liudīz (“people”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“man, people”). See the more common term, Leute (“people”).
From Old High German lispen (“lisp”) + -eln, ultimately from onomatopoeic Proto-Germanic *wlispaz (“stammering, lisping”).

From Middle High German lumpe. Lump (“cad”) is originally the same word. From Middle High German lunge, from Old High German lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungô (literally “the light organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Compare Dutch long, English lung, Danish lunge, Swedish lunga, Icelandic lunga.

From Middle High German lemen, lemmen, from Old High German lemmen, from Proto-Germanic *lamjaną, derived from *lamaz (“lame”), whence German lahm (“lame”). The simplification of the geminate and subsequent lengthening of the vowel by analogy with this underlying adjective.

Suffixed form in -ig of an older adjective lass (“languid, slothful, idle, weary”), from Old High German laȥ (“slow, sluggish”), from Proto-Germanic *lataz (“slow, weary”), from Proto-Indo-European *lad- (“slow, weary”). Akin to Old English læt (“slow, slack, lax, late”) (English late), Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐍄𐍃
From Middle High German lüften (“to lift into the air”), from Old High German luftēn, from Proto-Germanic *luftijaną. More at lift.

parole.significato: liar (one who tells lies) (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Old High German lugināri, derived from the noun lugina (“lie”), from Proto-Germanic *luginō, cognate with Old Saxon lugina, Old English lyġen, derived from the verb *leuganą (“to lie”). lügen + -er
From Middle High German lüzzel, lützel, from Old High German luzil, luzzil, liuzil, from Proto-Germanic *luttilaz, byform of *lūtilaz. Cognate with English little and Low German lütt.

parole.significato: lean, without fat (e.g. of meat or dairy)
parole.testo: From Old High German magar, from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Cognate with Dutch mager, Danish mager, Norwegian Bokmål mager, Norwegian Nynorsk mager, Swedish mager, etc., and with English meagre (through Indo-European via Latin and French).
From Middle High German māt, from Old High German *mād, from Proto-Germanic *mēþą.

parole.significato: to urge (someone) to do a specific, necessary task
parole.testo: From Middle High German mânen, from Old High German manōn, from Proto-Germanic *manōną. Cognate with Old English manian.

parole.significato: to grind loudly (the teeth, for example as part of the process of eating or as bruxism)
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *malmaz (“sand”), hence "to grind to sand".
From Middle High German malz, from Old High German malz, from Proto-Germanic *maltą (“malt”).
From Middle High German manecvaltec, from Old High German manicfaltīg, from Proto-Germanic *managafalþaz, equivalent to manch + faltig. Compare English manifold.

From Middle High German mate, matte, from Old High German *mata (attested in matoscrec (“grasshopper”)), from Proto-Germanic *maþwō or *madwō. Cognate with Middle Dutch and Middle Low German māde. Also related to English meadow (from Proto-Germanic *mēdwō).

From Middle High German mūl, mūle (“snout, mouth”), from Old High German *mūl, mūla (“snout”), from Proto-Germanic *mūlą, *mūlō (“muzzle, snout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“lips, muzzle”). From Old High German meist, from Proto-Germanic *maist, *maistaz. Compare Dutch meest, English most, Danish mest.
From Middle High German menige, from Old High German managī, from Proto-Germanic *managį̄ (compare English many, Swedish många). Equivalent to manch + -e.

parole.significato: mild (in all of its common senses)
parole.testo: From Middle High German milte, from Old High German milti. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German milde.

From Middle High German milze n, from Old High German milzi n, from Proto-Germanic *miltiją n. The feminine gender in modern German is from Middle Low German milte f, reinforced by the analogy with other inner organs. Cognate to Dutch milt, English milt.
From Middle High German minnen, from Old High German minneôn, minnôn, from Proto-Germanic *minjōną.

parole.significato: Same functions and meanings as the English prefix mis-; a nominal, adjectival and inseparable verbal prefix that negate…
parole.testo: From Middle High German mis-, misse-, from Old High German missa-, from Proto-Germanic *missa- (“wrongly, badly”).

From Middle High German missebrūchen, from Old High German missibrūchen, missibrūhhen, from Proto-Germanic *missabrūkaną, equivalent to miss- + brauchen. Cognate with German Low German missbruken, Dutch misbruiken, West Frisian misbrûke, Saterland Frisian misbruuke, Danish misbruge, Swedish missbruk
From Middle High German missen, from Old High German missan, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną.

From Middle High German missetāt, from Old High German mistāt, missitāt (“misdeed”), from Proto-Germanic *missadēdiz < *missa- (“mis-”) + *dēdiz (“deed, act”). Compare Dutch misdaad, West Frisian misdied, English misdeed, Danish misdåd, Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐍃𐍃𐌰𐌳𐌴𐌸𐍃 (missadēþs). More at misdeed.

From Middle High German mitte, from Old High German mitti, from Proto-Germanic *midjǭ (“centre”), *midją, from *midjaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo-. Cognate to Old Norse miðja and Old English midde, midd (English mid).

From Middle High German mittel, from Old High German mittil (akin to Old Saxon middil), from Proto-Germanic *midlą, *midilą, *medalą (“middle”), *midil-. Compare Dutch middel, English middle. See also Mitte.
Inherited from Middle High German mitternaht, from Old High German mittinaht, from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts.

From Middle High German molte, from Old High German molta, from Proto-Germanic *muldō.
From Middle High German mos, from Old High German mos, from Proto-Germanic *musą.

parole.testo: From Middle High German morgengābe, from Old High German morgangeba, Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō, equivalent to Morgen (“morning”) + Gabe (“gift”).

From Late Middle High German mugel (“lump, clod”), probably ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mūgô, from Proto-Indo-European *muk- (“heap”), similar to Ancient Greek μύκων (múkōn, “pile”). Germanic cognates include Old English mūga (“stack”), Old Norse múgi (“swathe, crowd”).

From Middle High German muotic, from Old High German muotag, from Proto-Germanic *mōdagaz; equivalent to Mut + -ig.

parole.testo: From Middle High German morder, mordære (also Middle High German morderære), from Old High German murdiro, murdreo (“murderer”), from Proto-Germanic *murþrijô (“murderer”). By surface analysis, morden + -er, or Mord + -er.

parole.significato: legally capable; mature; of age and not incapacitated; able to take independent legal and political decisions
parole.testo: From Middle High German mündec, derived from munt, from Proto-Germanic *mundō. Compare Vormund, mundtot.
From Old High German murwi, from Proto-Germanic *marwaz. Akin to English mellow, Dutch murw and Swedish mör.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlīkaz (“motherly, maternal”). By surface analysis, Mutter + -lich.

From Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh with preservation of word-final -h as -ch; thus pertaining to modern nah (“near”) (from Old High German inflected nāh-), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhw. Cognate with Dutch na, English nigh.

parole.significato: small boat used on inland waters
parole.testo: From Middle High German nache (“small boat”), from Old High German nahho, from Proto-Germanic *nakwô. Cognates include Dutch aak (“barque”), Old English naca and Old Norse nǫkkvi

From Middle High German nagen, from Old High German nagan, gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą. Cognate with English nag and gnaw.
From Middle High German nāme, from Old High German nāma, from Proto-Germanic *nēmō.
From Middle High German nāt, from Old High German nāt, from Proto-Germanic *nēdiz, derived from *nēaną (“to sew”), whence German nähen. Cognate with Dutch naad, Low German Nahd.

From Middle High German nëbel, from Old High German nëbul, from Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (whence also Proto-Balto-Slavic *nébas, Proto-Indo-Iranian *nábʰas, Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud, mist”), Latin nebula (“mist, fog”)). More at English nuel.

From Middle High German nīden, from Old High German nīdōn, from Proto-Germanic *nīþijaną.

parole.testo: From a merger of Middle High German nīgen (intransitive, strong) and neigen (transitive, weak), from Old High German nīgan and neigen, from Proto-Germanic *hnīganą and its causative *hnaigijaną. Cognate with Dutch nijgen and neigen, Old English hnīgan and Old English hnǣgan, Old Norse hnīga and hnei
From Middle High German netzen, from Old High German nezzen, from Proto-Germanic *natjaną (“to wetten”).
From Middle High German niunzëhen, from Old High German niunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun. Equivalent to neun + zehn. Compare Dutch negentien, English nineteen, Danish nitten.
From Middle High German nebel, from Old High German nibel (“mist”) + patronymic ending -ung, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *nebulaz + *-ungō.

From Middle High German niere (“kidney; testicle”) m, from Old High German nioro (“kidney; testicle”) m, from Proto-Germanic *neurô m, from Proto-Indo-European *négʷʰrō. From Middle High German nizze (13th c.), from the plural of older niz, from Old High German niz, from Proto-Germanic *hnits.

parole.testo: From Middle High German niches, nickes, from Old High German nihhus, nichus, from Proto-Germanic *nikwus, *nikwis, from Proto-Indo-European *nigʷ-ō-s, from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“wash”). Cognate with Old English nicor.

From Middle High German nixe, from Old High German nicchessa, feminine form of nichus, nihhus (“water-spirit”), from Proto-Germanic *nikwus, *nikwis, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“to wash”). More at nix, nicker.

From Middle High German notdurft, from Old High German notthurft. The first element is Not (“need”), while the second is obsolete Durft, which ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *þurftiz. Also compare dürftig (“sparse, meager”).

From Middle High German nuot, from Old High German nuot (“groove”), from the root of Proto-Germanic *hnōjaną (“to smooth, join together”), from Proto-Indo-European *kneh₂- (compare Ancient Greek κνάω (knáō, “to scratch, scrape”), whence English acnestis).

parole.significato: to make use of; to deploy; to exploit; to harness; to take (the opportunity of)
parole.testo: From Middle High German nutzen, nützen, from Old High German nuzzōn, -nuzzen (in ginuzzen), from Proto-Germanic *nutōną, *nutjōną, *nutjaną. Compare modern Nutzen (noun). From Old High German nabagēr, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz. Cognate with English auger, Dutch avegaar.
From Old High German nāhisto, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”). Compare Dutch naast, English next, Danish næste, Swedish nästa.
From Middle High German nāian, from Old High German nājen, nāian, from Proto-Germanic *nēaną. Cognate with German Nadel and English needle.

parole.significato: Introduces an indirect question, a doubt. if, whether.
parole.testo: From Middle High German obe, ob, from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”). Compare English if.

From Middle High German obe, from Old High German oba, from Proto-Germanic *ub (“under”), from Proto-Indo-European *upó (“under, below”). Related with über, oben. From Middle High German atel, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *adalaz. Cognate with English addle (“putrid”).

From Middle High German ofte, oft, uft, from Old High German ofta, ofto, oftu, from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”). Cognate with Dutch oft, English oft and often.

parole.testo: As a High German word from Middle High German urliuge, urlouge, urlage (“war”), from a merger of Old High German urliugi and urlag, respectively from Proto-Germanic *uzleugō (“war”) and *uzlagą (“destiny”). From Ost or Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą, related to *ausos (“dawn”), compare Latin aurora, and Latin auster, which, probably due to a re-orientation, means "South".

From Middle High German pfrieme, from Proto-Germanic *preumaz (compare Low German Preen, Dutch priem), alteration of *preunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *brewn- (compare Lithuanian briaunà (“edge”), Albanian brez (“belt, girdle”)). See English preen for reference.

parole.significato: tarpaulin, awning (large sheet of waterproof material used as covering)

From Middle High German bochen, puchen, from Proto-Germanic *puk-, which is probably imitative. Or, perhaps related to French poquer (“move in pétanque”).
From Middle High German braht, from Old High German braht, from Proto-Germanic *brahtaz.

parole.significato: to resplend, shine, to be shown, sported (to be highly visible)
parole.testo: From Middle High German prangen, brangen, probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *brahtaz, whence Pracht (“splendor”).

parole.significato: pillory; any construction to hold someone for public humiliation
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German pranger (13th c.), derived from *prangen, a West Central German form of phrengen, phrangen (“to force, squeeze, confine”), from Proto-Germanic *pranganą (compare English prong). Not related with prangen, but possibly at some point associated with it.

From Middle High German *britze (attested in derivatives, simplex 15th c.), from Old High German britissa (“thin plank”), derived from bret (Proto-Germanic *bredą, whence modern Brett) + -issa (Proto-Germanic *-isjō). From Middle High German buffen, sharing an imitative Proto-Germanic base with Old English pyffan, Middle English puffen, English puff. Compare also Middle Low German puffen, buffen, biffen, German Low German buffen (“to puff”).
From Old High German quedilla, from Proto-Germanic *kweþuz. Compare English kidney.
From Proto-Germanic *kwakōną (“to quack”), of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate with Dutch kwaken (“to croak”), English quack.
From Old High German questa, from Proto-Germanic *kwastuz.

From Middle High German ramme, from Old High German ramma (“battering ram”), from rammo (“ram, male sheep”) (whence now obsolete Ramm) from the similar shape of a ram's head, from Proto-Germanic *rammaz. See also Rammbock and Rammel.

parole.significato: edge, brink, rim (outer part of something)
parole.testo: From Middle High German rant, from Old High German rant, from Proto-Germanic *randō, which according to Duden is related to *hramō (“framework”). Pokorny prefers a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rem- (“to rest”). Cognate with English rand.

From an East Central German word for “sow on heat”, derived from Middle High German rangen (“to run back and forth”), from the root of Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to wring”). Related with wringen and rangeln (“to scrap, wrestle”). Note that the loss of initial w- in Range is simply the regular High G
From Middle High German ranc (“a quick turning movement”), from Old High German *rank, from Proto-Germanic *wrankiz (“a turn, twisting”). Cognate with English wrench.

From Middle High German rūch, from Old High German rūh, from Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz. Though etymologically justified, the silent h was abolished in 1996 because rauh was the only word in which it was used after the diphthong -au-. Cognate with Dutch ruig and ruw, English rough (which see).

From Middle High German rëche, Old High German rëhkho. Cognate with Middle Dutch rake, Old Norse reka (“rake”), Old English racu, Dutch reek (“rake”), English rake, Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (rikan, “to heap up, collect”). From Proto-Germanic *rakō, *rekô (“rake”).

From Middle High German rede, from Old High German redia, radia (“speech, view, opinion”), from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ, *raþjō (“accountability, speech”); from the same root as reden (“to talk, to speak”). parole.significato: to talk, to speak, to orate
parole.testo: From Middle High German reden, from Old High German redōn, rediōn (“to speak”), a derivative of reda, redia (“speech, word, opinion, view, mind”), from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ, *raþjō (“accountability, speech”). See Rede.
From Middle High German redenære, from Old High German redināri, derived from the verb redinōn, a lost byform of redōn (whence reden). Now analysable as reden + -ner.

parole.significato: a rack of shelves, shelving, a shelf (in this collective sense), e.g. an open bookcase
parole.testo: Early 17th century, of unclear origin. Hypotheses include: * Derived from Proto-Germanic *rigǭ ~ *rīgǭ ~ *rīhǭ, whence German Riege and Reihe (both originally “row, line”). * Derived from Latin rēgula, whence German Riegel (“bar, latch”), Dutch richel (“bar, latch”, dialectally also “rack”). In both
From Middle High German regentropfe, from Old High German regantropfo, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to Regen + Tropfen.
From Old High German reganwazzar, from Proto-Germanic *regnawatōr. Equivalent to Regen (“rain”) + Wasser (“water”).
From Middle High German rīchtuom, from Old High German rīhhituom, rīhtuom, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijadōmaz, equivalent to reich + -tum. Cognate with Hunsrik Reichdum, Dutch rijkdom, English richdom.

From Middle High German rīmen (“to compose, put into verse, rhyme”), from Old High German rīman (“to count, enumerate”), from Proto-Germanic *rīmaną (“to count”). Cognate with Middle Low German rîmen (“to appraise, show honour, put into verse, rhyme”).

parole.significato: to irritate (to cause or induce displeasure or irritation)
parole.testo: Middle High German reizen, Old High German reiʒen, Proto-Germanic *raitijaną

parole.significato: to run; to race; to sprint (said of competing sportsmen, animals etc.)
parole.testo: From a merger of transitive / causative Old High German rennan (“to make something run or flow”) (from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną), and intransitive Old High German rinnan (“to run or flow”) (from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną). A similar development of merging roots can be seen in Dutch rennen and English

parole.significato: Riesling grape (a variety of grape grown especially in Germany and other relatively cool areas)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from a Middle High German variant of rueszling, perhaps ruoz (“soot”), from Old High German hruoz, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”) + the suffix -ling. The semantic connection with soot would be referring to the grapes' tendency to develop black spots when ripe. There are sev

parole.significato: to groove (provide with narrow, parallel channels)
parole.testo: From Middle High German riffeln, rifilen, from Old High German riffilōn (“to ripple, remove seeds from flax”), derived from riffila (“ripple”), from Proto-Germanic *ripilō, which is probably related to *rīpaną (“to harvest, reap”). Cognate with Dutch repel, English ripple. The sense “to cut grooves
From Middle High German rinne, from Old High German rinna, from Proto-Germanic *rinnǭ.
From rinnen (“to trickle”) + -sal (abstract noun suffix). Possibly from Proto-Germanic *rannislō and cognate with Icelandic rennsli (“run, leak”).
From Middle High German riss, from Old High German riz, from Proto-Germanic *writiz.
From Middle High German rist, from Old High German rist, from Proto-Germanic *wristuz. Compare English wrist.
From Middle High German rite, from Old High German rito (“fever”), from a stem variant of Proto-Germanic *hriþiz (literally “trembling”). Archaic since the 17th century, now entirely unused.

From Middle High German rogen and roge, from Old High German rogan, rogin, *hrogan and rogo (“roe”), from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz and *hrugô (“roe”). Of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“frogspawn”). Compare Low German Rögen, Dutch roge, English roe, Danish rogn. More at r
From Middle High German rostec, from Old High German rostag, from Proto-Germanic *rustagaz (“rusty”), equivalent to Rost (“rust”) + -ig (“-y”). Cognate with English rusty.
From Proto-Germanic *hruttōną (“to snore, roar”), attested since the 16th century, synchronically analyzable as Rotz + -en.

parole.significato: heinous, nefarious, profane, unholy, blasphemous, infamous, wicked, abominable
parole.testo: From Middle High German ruochlōs, ruochelōs, rūchelōs, from Old High German ruochalōs, ruohhalōs, from Proto-Germanic *rōkōlausaz, *rōkijalausaz, cognate with English reckless.

parole.significato: to row (propel over water using oars)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ruodern, from Old High German ruoderōn, garuoderōn, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *rōaną (“to row”). Also see Ruder.

parole.significato: stanchion (vertical stake on a wagon used to fix the load)
parole.testo: From Middle High German runge, from Old High German hrunga, from Proto-Germanic *hrungō. Cognate with Dutch rong, English rung, Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐌿𐌲𐌲𐌰 (hrugga).
From Middle High German ruoȥ, rūȥ, from Old High German ruoȥ, hruoȥ, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”), from Proto-Indo-European *kreH(u)d-.
From Middle High German ruote, from Old High German ruota, from Proto-Germanic *rōdō. Akin to Old Saxon rōda, compare Hunsrik Rut, Dutch roede and English rod and rood (“cross”).

15th century, iterative extension of obsolete räuchen, from Middle High German röuchen, byform of rouchen, whence modern German rauchen (“to smoke”), which see for more. Both from Proto-Germanic *raukijaną. By surface analysis, Rauch + -ern. Compare Luxembourgish reecheren, Hunsrik reichre.

parole.significato: male dog (male dog, wolf or fox, as opposed to a bitch (often attributive), also used for certain other mammals)
parole.testo: From Middle High German rüde, rüd, from Old High German rudio, from Proto-Germanic *hruþjô (“male dog”), possibly from *hruttōn- (“to roar”), from a Proto-Indo-European root shared by Ancient Greek κόρυζα (kóruza), Old English hrot. Or, from Proto-Germanic *hreutan-, *hrūtan-, *hruttōną (“to snore”)

parole.significato: to reprimand, to criticize (to convey one's disapproval of someone due to their behavior, often formally but without fu…
parole.testo: From Middle High German rüegen, from Old High German ruogen, from Proto-Germanic *wrōgijaną.

parole.significato: to salt (something) for flavor; to season
parole.testo: From Middle High German salzen, from Old High German salzan, from Proto-Germanic *saltaną.
From Middle High German soufen (“to drink, slurp, sink, go down”), from Old High German sūfan, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną. Cognate with Dutch zuipen, Swedish supa (Old Norse súpa), English sup.

parole.significato: scraper, flat instrument with a handle used for scraping
parole.testo: From Middle High German schabe (“scraper, chaff, moulding; moth, cockroach”), from Old High German scaba (“scraper, plane”), from Proto-Germanic *skabō (“scraper”). Cognate with Dutch schaaf (“plane”). Also related to German Low German Schabbe (“mange, scabies”), English scab.

parole.significato: yarrow (any of several pungent Eurasian herbs, of the genus Achillea)
parole.testo: From Schaf (“sheep”) + Garbe (“yarrow”). The second element may derive from Old High German garwa, garawa, from Proto-Germanic *garwo; see Garbe (“yarrow”). Compare Dutch gerw, English yarrow.
From Middle High German schāle, from Old High German scāla, from Proto-Germanic *skēlō, related to *skaljō (“husk, shell”). Cognate with Dutch schaal (“bowl”).
From Middle High German schar, from Old High German scaro. Cognate with German scheren (“to shear”), German Schere (“shear, scissors”), English share (“plowshare”), English shear.

From Middle High German scharte f, also schart f or m, from the adjective Old High German *scart (“wounded, cut up”, attested in liduscart), from Proto-Germanic *skardaz. Related with German scheren (“to shear”). Cognate with Middle Dutch schaert m, Middle Low German schārt n, Old English sceard n,
From Middle High German schūfele, schūvele, from Old High German scūvala, from Proto-Germanic *skuflō. Cognate with English shovel.

From Middle High German schelle, from Old High German scella, from Proto-Germanic *skellǭ (“bell”), from Proto-Indo-European *skel- (“to sound; resound; ring”); see the related schellen (“to ring”) for more.

parole.significato: to scold (someone); to rebuke; to chide
parole.testo: From Middle High German schëlten, from Old High German skëltan, from Proto-Germanic *skeldaną. Compare English scold.

parole.significato: an indistinct shape or shadow; a silhouette in the dark, in mist, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle High German scheme m or f, from Old High German *skemo m, skema f, from Proto-Germanic *skīmô, *skimô, *skimō. From Middle High German scherbe, from Old High German scirbi, from Proto-Germanic *skarbōjan-, related to *skrapōną (“to scratch”).

parole.significato: widow's mite, i.e. a small donation or contribution, esp. of monetary kind.
parole.testo: Diminutive of Scherf, from Middle High German scherf, scherpf (“a coin of small value, esp. a halfpenny”), from Old High German scerf, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skrapōną (“to scratch”). Related to modern Scherbe (“shard”) and Middle High German scharben (“to notch, to nick”) (from Old High Ger

parole.significato: to joke; to jest; to frolic
parole.testo: From Middle High German schërzen, from Old High German *skërzan (“to jump merrily, enjoy oneself, jest”), from Proto-Germanic *skertaną.

From Middle High German schiune, from Old High German scugin(n)a, from a Proto-Germanic *sku(w)enjō-, for which see Proto-Germanic *skūrō (“shelter, shack”) for more. Derived from Proto-Germanic *skarną (“dung”) due to the plant’s preferred habitat. Compare dialectal English sh

parole.significato: sailor; skipper (one who navigates a ship or boat, or works on it, especially in inland navigation)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schiffære, schiffere, from Old High German *skiffāri, from Proto-Germanic *skipārijaz (“sailor”). Doublet of Schipper and Skipper.
From Middle High German schillinc, from Old High German skilling, from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz.

From Middle High German schinden, schinten (“to cheat; swindle; torment; peel off; skin”), from Old High German skinden, skinten (“to skin; flay; peel off”), derived from the noun Middle High German schint (“fruit peel”), all ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skinþą (“fruit peel”). Cognate with German

parole.significato: to slaughter (kill livestock; kill people brutally)
parole.testo: From Middle High German slahten, from Old High German slahtōn (“slaughter, sacrifice”), from Proto-Germanic *slahtōną, related to *slahaną (“to hit, strike”). Cognate with Dutch slachten.

From Middle High German slaf, from Old High German slaf, from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”). The same word of Low German origin is schlapp, a synonym in modern standard German.

From Middle High German slange, from Old High German slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô. Cognate with German Low German Slang (“snake”), Dutch slang (“snake”), West Frisian slang (“snake”). Compare also Albanian shlligë (“adder”).
From Middle High German slanc, Middle Low German slank, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist, wind”), the source of schlingen.

parole.significato: bad, evil, wicked (the opposite of good; immoral)
parole.testo: From earlier slecht, from Middle High German slëht, from Old High German slëht (see also schlicht), from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz. Cognate with English slight, Dutch slecht, Afrikaans sleg, Icelandic sléttur, Faroese slættur, Swedish slätt, Danish slet, Gothic 𐍃𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (slaihts), and Norwegian slett.
From Middle High German slīm, from Old High German slīm, from Proto-Germanic *slīmą. Cognate with Dutch slijm, English slime.

From Middle High German lenderen, from Old High German landteri, from Proto-Germanic *land-, ultimately from the root of schlingen (“to wind, twist, coil”). Cognate with Dutch slenteren (“to loiter”).

parole.significato: to hurl; to fling; to sling
parole.testo: From Middle High German slūdern, perhaps ultimately from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Related to schludern and schlottern.
From Middle High German slich, from Old High German slich, from Proto-Germanic *slīką. Doublet of Schleich and Schlick.

parole.significato: sled, sledge, sleigh (any vehicle moving over snow or ice on parallel skids)
parole.testo: From Middle High German slite, from Old High German slito, from Proto-Germanic *slidô. Cognate with Luxembourgish Schlitt, Dutch slee, English sled and sleigh, Swedish släde, Icelandic sleði, Italian slitta.

Middle High German slotern, intensive form of sloten (“to tremble, hang down loosely”). Perhaps related to a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber.

parole.significato: to work sloppily, carelessly, without proper concentration or commitment
parole.testo: From Middle High German slūdern (“to sway”), related with schleudern (“to swing, hurl”). Perhaps ultimately from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Compare also Dutch slodderen (“to be sloppy”). From Middle High German slüpfen, slupfen, from Old High German *slupfen, from Proto-Germanic *slupjaną, related to *sleupaną (“to slip, sneak”).

From Middle High German slipferec, from Old High German sleffarag (influenced by Old High German slipfīg), from Old High German sleffar (“slippery”), from Proto-Germanic *slipraz (“slippery”). Figurative sense from 17th c.
From Middle High German smāch, smāhe, from Old High German smāhi (“small”), from Proto-Germanic *smēhaz.

parole.significato: narrow, slender (not wide, comparatively long), small
parole.testo: From Middle High German smal, from Old High German smal, from Proto-Germanic *smalaz. Cognate with Dutch smal, Low German small, English small.

From Middle High German smæhen, from Old High German smāhen, from Proto-Germanic *smēhijaną (“to reduce; belittle; despise”), from Proto-Indo-European *smēyg- (“small, thin, delicate”). See also Dutch smaad (“slander”), Proto-Germanic *smikraz (“fine, fair”), Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“little”).

From Middle High German snabel, from Old High German snabul, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz (“snout, muzzle”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksnew- (“to scratch, rub”). Cognate with Dutch snavel, Saterland Frisian Snoabel (“beak, bill”), Old English snofl (“mucus, snivel”).

parole.significato: to utter a croaky sound, to snar, to snarl, to squawk
parole.testo: From Middle High German snarren, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *snarkōną, of imitative origin (lautmalend). Compare Middle Low German snarren, snarren, English snar, snarl, German schnurren.

parole.significato: snow-white, white as snow, pure white
parole.testo: From Middle High German snēwīz, from Old High German *snēwīz, from Proto-Germanic *snaiwahwītaz, equivalent to Schnee + weiß.

parole.significato: keelback slug (any of various slugs of the family Limacidae)
parole.testo: From Middle High German snegel (“slug, snail”), from Old High German snegil, from Proto-Germanic *snagilaz. Cognate with Low German Snagel, English snail. The word failed to establish itself in Modern Standard German, but was later adopted in a more specialized sense in zoological terminology.

parole.significato: to sniff up snot through the nose
parole.testo: First attested in the 17th century as schnieben, a Central German variant of schnauben. The form with f is analogous to schnaufen, which compare. parole.significato: to carve (e.g. a figure, usually out of wood)
parole.testo: From Middle High German snitzen, from Proto-Germanic *snittōną (“to cut”).
From Middle High German snuor, from Old High German snuor, from Proto-Germanic *snōrō. Cognate with Dutch snoer. Also related to English snare.

parole.significato: to blow one's nose (to expel mucus from nose)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sniuzen, from Old High German snūzen, snūzōn, from Proto-Germanic *snūtijaną. From Middle High German snoede, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *snauþuz (“bald, naked, poor”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksnéw-tu-s, from the root *ksnew- (“to scrape, sharpen”). Cognates include Dutch snood, sneu and Old Norse snauðr.

From Middle High German snüeren, from Old High German *snuoren (in firsnuoren), possibly from Proto-Germanic *snōrijaną, from *snōrō, whence German Schnur. Cognate with Dutch and Middle Dutch snoeren, Middle Low German snȫren, Old Norse snœra.
From Middle High German schober, from Old High German scobar, itself from the Proto-Germanic stem *skup- (“barn, shed”), from which also Schopf, Schuppen and English shop.
From Middle High German schorf, from Old High German scorf (in compounds), from Proto-Germanic *skurf-, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”) Compare English scurf, scurvy, scruffy.

parole.significato: lap (area between the waist and knees of a seated person)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schōȥ, schōȥe, from Old High German scōȥo, from Proto-Germanic *skautaz. Compare Dutch schoot, Icelandic skaut, Danish skød ("lap", "womb").

From Middle High German schōte (“pod; pea”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *skaudō (“sheath, husk”), which is probably related to *hūdijaną (“to conceal”). Cognate with Middle Low German schōde, Old Norse skauð, and perhaps the first element in Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍀𐍃 (skaudaraips).

parole.significato: gate (barrier that can be pulled or moved up to allow passage)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schranke, related to Old High German firskrenken (“to prevent”), German schränken (“to put or pile things crosswise”), from Proto-Germanic *skrankaz (“barrier, grid”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”).
Inherited from Middle High German schrat, from Old High German scrato, from Proto-Germanic *skrattuz.

From Middle High German schrōt, from Old High German scrōt, from Proto-Germanic *skraudō.

From Middle High German schupfen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. Doublet of now colloquial German schuppen. Also cognate with schubsen and Dutch schoppen. See also Bavarian schupfn.
From Middle High German schuor, schür, from Old High German *skuora, from Proto-Germanic *skōrō (“shearing”). Cognate with Old English scora (“a hairy garment”).

parole.significato: swarm of insects; flock of birds; school of fish
parole.testo: From Middle High German swarm, from Old High German swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”). Compare Dutch zwerm, English swarm, Danish sværm. The sense “crush” is a backformation from the verb schwärmen; see there.

From Middle High German swarte, Old High German *swarta, from Proto-Germanic *swarduz (“rind, tough skin”). Cognate with Middle English sward, West Frisian swarde, Old Norse svǫrðr, Old English sweard, Danish svær, Dutch zwoerd, English sward, Gothic *𐍃𐍅𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (*swardus).
From Middle High German swëben, from Old High German swëbēn, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną (“to move”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksweybʰ- (“to twist, turn around”).

parole.significato: sulfur, brimstone (chemical element, S, atomic number 16)
parole.testo: From Middle High German swevel, from Old High German sweval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz; cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌹𐌱𐌻𐍃 (swibls).

From Middle High German sweiz, from Old High German sweiz, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, *swaitaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), *sweyd-. Cognate with German Low German Sweet, Dutch zweet, English sweat, West Frisian swit, Danish sved, and Yiddish שוויצן (shvitsn); see sweat for more
From Middle High German sweiʒen, sweizen (“to roast, to weld”), from Old High German sweizen (“to roast”), from Proto-Germanic *swaitijaną, causative of etymology 2.

From Middle High German sweizen (“to sweat, bleed”), from Old High German *sweizan, from Proto-Germanic *swaitaną. Cognate with Luxembourgish schweessen (“to sweat”), Dutch zweten (“to sweat”), English sweat.
From Middle High German swëlgen, from Old High German swëlgan, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą (“to gulp (down); swallow; devour”). Cognate with Old English swelgan (English swallow).
From Middle High German swëllen, from Old High German swëllan, from Proto-Germanic *swellaną. Compare Low German swellen, Dutch zwellen, English swell, Swedish svälla.
From Middle High German swëllen, from Old High German *swellen (only attested in biswellen), from Proto-Germanic *swallijaną, causative verb of *swellaną.

parole.significato: to wash (move by the current of water)
parole.testo: From Middle High German swemmen, from Old High German *swemmen, from Proto-Germanic *swammijaną. Equivalent to a causative of schwimmen, thus originally “to make swim or float”. Cognate with Old English beswemman.
From Middle High German swiger, from Old High German swigar, from Proto-Germanic *swegrō.

Expanded from earlier Schwieger (“mother-in-law”), from Old High German swigar, from Proto-Germanic *swegrō, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱruh₂- (“woman's mother-in-law”) (compare *swéḱuros (“woman's father-in-law”)). By surface analysis, schwieger- + Mutter.

parole.significato: to swing (to move back and forth)
parole.testo: From Middle High German swingen, from Old High German swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą. Cognate with Low German swingen, English swing. Doublet of swingen.
From Middle High German swulst f (“tumor, growth”), from swellen (“to swell up, bulge”), from Old High German swellan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”).
From Middle High German swuor, from Old High German swuor, from Proto-Germanic *swōraz (“oath”), from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”). Compare English swear and Vilamovian śwür.

From Middle High German sweher, from Old High German swehur, from Proto-Germanic *swehuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros. Cognate with Old English swēor, Latin socer and Ancient Greek ἑκυρός (hekurós).
From Old High German swero, from Proto-Germanic *swerô, a nominal formation from *sweraną (“to hurt, ulcerate”).

parole.significato: to fester, to suppurate, to ulcerate and to hurt
parole.testo: From Middle High German swërn, from Old High German swëran, from Proto-Germanic *sweraną.

parole.significato: beauty, the quality of being beautiful
parole.testo: From Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōnī, from Proto-Germanic *skaunį̄. Analysable as schön + -e.

With sporadic rounding after sch from Middle High German schiter, from Old High German skitir, sketar, with regular preservation of t before r from Proto-Germanic *skit(a)raz. Cognate with Ancient Greek σκιδαρός (skidarós, “thin, fine, weak”). The word was widely obsolete in standard German until th

From Middle High German schütze, from Old High German scuzzo, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, *skuttijaną (“to bar, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *skuttą, *skuttjō (“bar, bolt, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”). Compare English shut.
From Old High German sehsto, from Proto-Germanic *sehstô. Equivalent to sechs + -te.

From Middle High German seh(s)zehen, from Old High German seh(s)zehan, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun. Equivalent to sechs + zehn. Compare Dutch zestien, West Frisian sechstjin, English sixteen, Danish seksten.
From Middle High German seh(s)zec, from Old High German sehszug, from Proto-Germanic *sehs tigiwiz. Equivalent to sechs + -zig.

15th century, alteration of Seelhund, explanatory compound from now obsolete Seel (“seal”) + Hund (“dog”). The first component seems to have been inherited from Middle High German sële, sëleh, from Old High German sëlah, from Proto-Germanic *selhaz (“seal”). For natural reasons it was a rare word, h

From Middle High German seife, from Old High German seifa, seiffa, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, dribble, strain, trickle”). Cognate with Dutch zeep, Low German Seep, West Frisian sjippe, English soap.
From Middle High German sīt, from Old High German sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīþuz. Akin to Old Saxon sīd, Old English sīþ. Related to Dutch sedert and sinds.

parole.significato: side (a bounding straight edge of a two-dimensional shape)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sît(e), from Old High German sīta, from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ. Cognate with Dutch zijde, Low German Siede, English side, Swedish sida.
From Middle High German selp, from Old High German selb, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz. More at self.

With excrescent -t (same: eins > einst, su(n)s > sonst etc.) fossilized from the neutral gendered Middle High German sëlbes, from the Old High German pronoun sëlb, sëlbo, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”), from *s(w)e- (“separate, apart”). Compare Low German
From Old High German senken, from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną. Causative of sinken.

parole.significato: armchair, easy chair (comfortable chair with supports for the arms or elbows)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sëȥȥel, from Old High German sëȥȥal, from Proto-Germanic *setlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”). Cognates include English settle, Dutch zetel, Gothic 𐍃𐌹𐍄𐌻𐍃 (sitls).

From Middle High German sibenzehen, from Old High German sibunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Equivalent to sieben + zehn. Compare Dutch zeventien, West Frisian santjin, English seventeen, Danish sytten.
From Middle High German sibenzec, from Old High German sibunzug, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą. Equivalent to sieben + -zig. Cognate with Hunsrik sibzich.
From Middle High German sieden, from Old High German siodan, from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną.
From Old High German silberīn, from Proto-Germanic *silubrīnaz.

From Middle High German sinder, from Old High German sintar, from Proto-Germanic *sindraz (“dross, cinder, slag”), from Proto-Indo-European *sendʰro- (“coagulating fluid, liquid slag, scale, cinder”). For the consonantism, see hinter. Related with Dutch sintel, Middle Low German sinder, sinter, West

From Middle High German sōr, from Old High German *sōr, from Proto-Germanic *sauzaz (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂ews- (“dry, parched”) (also reconstructed as *h₂sews-). Cognate with Dutch zoor (“dry, rough”) and English sear.
From Middle High German sulich, from Old High German sulīh, from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz.
From Proto-Germanic *sundraz (“separate, isolated, alone”).
From Middle High German sunder, from Old High German suntar, from Proto-Germanic *sundraz (“isolated, particular, alone”).
From Middle High German sundern, from Old High German suntarōn (“separate, distinguish”), from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną (“to sunder, to separate”). Cognate with English sunder, Dutch zonderen.

parole.significato: to take care of, to care for, to look after
parole.testo: From Middle High German sorgen, from Old High German sorgēn, from Proto-Germanic *surgāną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”). Cognate with English sorrow.

parole.significato: span (space between the tips of the thumb and little finger)
parole.testo: From Middle High German spanne, from Old High German spanna, from Proto-Germanic *spannō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to stretch”). Cognate with Dutch span, spanne, English span.
From Middle High German spannen, from Old High German spannan, from Proto-Germanic *spannaną.
From Middle High German sparre, from Old High German sparro, from Proto-Germanic *sparrô.
From Middle High German spitze, from Old High German spizza, from Proto-Germanic *spitjaz, related to *spitō (“spike”). Compare English spit (“skewer”), Swedish spets (“point, tip; lace”).

parole.significato: a speaker; one who speaks (male or unspecified sex); especially:
parole.testo: From Middle High German sprecher, sprechære, from Old High German sprechāri, sprehhāri (also as sprāchāri, sprāhhāri), an alteration (with change of suffix) of Old High German sprecho, sprehho, from Proto-Germanic *sprekô (“speaker”), equivalent to sprechen + -er. Compare English speaker.

parole.significato: to spring; to leap; to bounce
parole.testo: From Old High German springan, from Proto-Germanic *springaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sprenǵʰ-. Compare Low German springen, Dutch springen, West Frisian springe, English spring, Danish springe.

parole.significato: to spurt, to squirt, to splash, to spatter, to spray
parole.testo: From Middle High German sprützen (“to squirt”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sprittōną (“to disperse”).
From Middle High German spuole, from Old High German spuola, spuolo, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ, *spōlô (“spool”). More at spool.

parole.significato: trace (rest of something that indicates its former presence; (by extension) any small amount)
parole.testo: From Middle High German spur, spor (usually n, also rarely m and f), from Old High German spor, *spur, from Proto-Germanic *spurą n. Cognate to Dutch spoor, whence (through Afrikaans) English spoor.
From Middle High German spehen, from Old High German spehōn, spiohōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

parole.significato: to sense, to detect, to perceive
parole.testo: From Middle High German spüren, spuren, spurn, from Old High German spurien, spurren, from Proto-Germanic *spurjaną. By surface analysis, Spur + -en. Cognate with dialectal English speer, Scots speir, Swedish spörja.

parole.significato: pole; bar; rod; post (a long stick, usually round and of metal, but also of other material, especially when fixed somew…
parole.testo: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German stanga, from Proto-Germanic *stangō. Compare English stang.

parole.significato: to press; to punch; to stamp
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *stantōną, related to *stuntaz (“short, stunted”).

parole.significato: a cylindrical or slightly conical drinking vessel without a stem, typically with no handle, beaker
parole.testo: From Middle High German stouf, from Old High German stouf, from Proto-Germanic, existing as a drinking vessel name as well in Middle Low German stōp, Old English stēap, English stoup, Old Norse staup.

From Middle High German stīc, from Old High German stīg, from Proto-Germanic *stīgaz (“path”), related to German steigen. Cognate with Old English stīġ (“path; footpath; narrow way”), English sty (“ladder”), Danish sti, Norwegian Bokmål sti.

From Middle High German steige, from Old High German steiga, from Proto-Germanic *staigō. Related with (but not identical to) more usual Steig, Stieg m, from Middle High German stīc. Related with steigen.

From Middle High German stīge, from Old High German stīga (“pigsty”). Cognate with Old Saxon stīga (“pigsty”), whence the modern doublet Stiege (“wooden crate”). Possibly a byform of Proto-Germanic *stiją, whence English sty, but definitely related with it.

From Middle High German stelze, from Old High German stelza, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *staltijǭ, which is related to *stalljan (“to place, put”). Cognate with Middle Low German stelte, Dutch stelt, English stilt.
From Old High German sterz, from Proto-Germanic *stertaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)terd-, from *(s)ter- (“to be stiff”).

parole.significato: always; constantly; the whole time (very often)
parole.testo: From Middle High German stetes, from Proto-Germanic *stēdi-; cognate with Dutch steeds. Synchronically analyzed as an adverbial formation stet (“steady, constant”) + -s; see there for more.

From stief- (“step-”) + Tochter (“daughter”). From Middle High German stieftohter, from Old High German stioftohter, from Proto-Germanic *steupaduhtēr (“stepdaughter”), equivalent to stief- + Tochter.

parole.significato: narrow, often steep stairs (e.g. to a loft)
parole.testo: From Middle High German stiege, from Old High German stiega, a variant (with an unusual ablaut grade) of Proto-Germanic *stigǭ (“path, way, staircase, ladder”). Related with German steigen and English stair. See also Bavarian Stiagn.
From Middle High German stier (“bull”), from Old High German stior (“bull, calf of a bull”), from Proto-Germanic *steuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros.

From the verbalization of Stier (“bull”), due to the stare of a bull, from Middle High German stier (“bull”), from Old High German stior (“bull, calf of a bull”). From Proto-Germanic *steuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros.
From Middle High German stinken, from Old High German stinkan, stincan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną. Compare Dutch stinken, English stink.

parole.significato: to stop, to attain stagnation or cease to proceed
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *stukkōną (“to stop, stick”). Though a surface analysis as Stock (“stick, broken-off twig”) + -en (“infinitive suffix”), as suggested by Pfeiffer, is not exactly correct, said analysis does trace back to the same root as *stukkōną.

parole.significato: gallery; tunnel (long cavity in rock, usually man-made, but sometimes natural)
parole.testo: From Middle High German stolle, from Old High German stollo (“prop, post”), from Proto-Germanic *stullô (“support, post”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”).
From Middle High German stolz, from Old High German stolz, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz (“proud, stately, stiff”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, stand”); cognate with English stout.
From Middle High German stolz, from Old High German stolz, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz (“proud, stately, stiff”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, stand”); cognate with English stout.

From Middle High German strac (“straight”), from Old High German *strac (attested in framstrac), from Proto-Germanic *strakkaz (“straight”), from Proto-Indo-European *streg-, *treg- (“stiff, rigid”). Cognate with Dutch strak. More at stretch.
From Middle High German strāfen, most likely from Proto-Germanic *strēpōną (see Strafe (“punishment”)). Cognate with Luxembourgish strofen, Dutch straffen.
From Middle High German strant, from Old High German *strand, from Proto-Germanic *strandō. Cognate with English strand (“shore; beach”). More at strand.

From Middle High German strank, stranc, strange, from Old High German stranc, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ-; related to Middle High German strange f, from Old High German stranga (“strand”). Cognate with Low German Strenge, Dutch streng, English string, Danish str

parole.significato: a kind of fritter or doughnut
parole.testo: From Middle High German strūbe, from the adjective Proto-Germanic *strūbaz (“stiff, shaggy”). Doublet of northern Struwe (“kind of pancake”). Further cognate with Dutch struif.

parole.significato: [auxiliary haben] to brush, to graze, to stroke
parole.testo: From Middle High German streifen, from Old High German *streifen (in abastreifen > modern abstreifen), from Proto-Germanic *straipijaną, *stripōną (“to touch”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Pokorny derives the word from Proto-Indo-European *ster-, *strē- (“strip, streak”), for which see Strahl (“be

From Middle High German strenge, from Old High German strengi (“strong”), strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangijaz (“tight, tense”), *strangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut”); related to Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“stiff”). Cognate with Dutch streng, English strong, Danish streng.

From strudeln, from Middle High German strëden, from Old High German strëdan (“to burn, glow, hiss, whiz”), from Proto-Germanic *streþaną (“to burn, seethe, whirl”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to stream, flow, run”).

parole.significato: stocking; hose (women’s undergarment covering the foot, the lower leg, and part of the thigh)
parole.testo: From Middle High German strumpf, from Proto-Germanic *strumpaz (“stem, stalk”). The semantic shift from "stalk, stump" to "leg clothing" came about as a result of a fashion development, where originally one-piece leg garments were separated into two parts, the trousers and the socks. The socks were
From Middle High German stumpf, stump, from Old High German stumpf, stumph, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz (“stump, blunt, part cut off”). Cognate with English stump.
From Middle High German stuot, from Old High German stuot (“herd of horses”), from Proto-Germanic *stōdą.
From Middle High German stürmen, from Old High German sturmen, from Proto-Germanic *sturmijaną. Equivalent to Sturm + -en.

parole.significato: broth, stock, brew (liquid that remains after cooking, boiling)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sut, from Old High German *sut, from Proto-Germanic *sudą (“brew, soup”); related to sieden (“to boil”). Cognate with Old English ġesod (“cooking, boiling, seething”), Old Frisian soth (“cooking, boiling”), Danish sod, Icelandic soð.

parole.significato: to wash, to work in the scullery
parole.testo: From Middle High German sudelen, derived Middle High German sudel (“puddle”) + -en, a noun still known in the 20th century as Sudel m, from Proto-Germanic *seud- (“mud; soil”), from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“moisture”). Cognate with Old English gesyd (“wallow”).
From Proto-Germanic *sumpaz. Cognate with English swamp and sump.

parole.significato: a thin shaving or chip of wood produced during sawing
parole.testo: Equivalent to Säge or sägen + Span; ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sagōspēnuz. Compare Plautdietsch Soagespoon n, Swedish sågspån, Faroese saguspønir m pl (“sawdust”).
From obsolete süpfeln, an iterative formation of obsolete supfen, from Middle High German supfen (“to slurp”), from Old High German sūfan, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną. Doublet of saufen.
From Middle High German süene, suone, from Old High German suona, from Proto-Germanic *swōnō. Cognate with Dutch zoen (“kiss”).

parole.significato: food, usually meat or fish, in aspic
parole.testo: From Middle High German sülze, from Old High German sulza, from Proto-Germanic *sultijō (“salt water, brine”). Compare Dutch zult.
From Middle High German sunde, from Old High German sunta, from Proto-Germanic *sundī. Compare Dutch zonde, English sin, Danish synd.
From Middle High German sünder, sündære, sündāre, suntære, suntāre, from Old High German suntāri, from Proto-Germanic *sundārijaz, equivalent to Sünde + -er. More at sinner.
From Old High German suozen, from Proto-Germanic *swōtijaną, derived from *swōtuz (“sweet”), whence German süß (“sweet”).

parole.significato: mat (a flat piece of coarse material used for wiping one’s feet, or as a decorative or protective floor covering)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tacke, from Old High German tacha, from Proto-Germanic *dakkōną, related to Proto-Germanic *dōkaz (“cloth, rag”). Compare Bavarian Tackn, Dackn.

From Middle High German tagewerc, tagewerch, from Old High German tagawerk, from Proto-Germanic *dagawerką. Cognate with English daywork. Equivalent to Tag + Werk. The measure of land corresponds to the area that can be ploughed in a day by a team of oxen.

parole.significato: brave, dauntless, hardy, tough (strong in the face of hardship, pain, danger)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tapfer, from Old High German tapfar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz.

From Middle High German tasche, from Old High German taska, tasca. Further origin unknown. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Cognate with Dutch tas, Hunsrik Tasch, Middle Low German tasche (“bag, pouch”), Old Norse taska (“bag, purse”) (probably borrowed from Low German). Compare English tasse (“p

Ultimately probably from Proto-Germanic *taltrōną, *taltōną (“to sway, dangle, hesitate”), from Proto-Indo-European *del-, *dul- (“to shake, hesitate”). Compare Dutch touteren (“to tremble”), English dodder, Norwegian dialectal totra (“to quiver, shake”).

From Middle High German tou, from Old High German tou, from Proto-Germanic *dawwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”). Compare Low German Dau, Dutch dauw, English dew, compare also Danish dug.

From Middle High German tougen, tugen, tügen, from Old High German tugan (attested since the 9th century); from Proto-Germanic *duganą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to produce”). Germanic cognates include Yiddish טויגן (toygn), Old Saxon dugan, Dutch deugen (> Afrikaans deug), Old English dug

parole.significato: dough, paste, pastry, batter (soft, at least partially cohesive mixture of ingredients, often including flour, intended…
parole.testo: From Middle High German teic, from Old High German teig, teic (attested since the 9th century); from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, to mold, to form”). Cognate with English dough, Dutch deeg, Old English dāg, Old Norse deig (whence Icelandic deig, Faroese deigg

From Old High German turran, from Proto-Germanic *durzaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰers-. Cognate with Low German dören, English dare, but also with Ancient Greek θρασύς (thrasús), Lithuanian drįsti, Russian дерза́ть (derzátʹ).

From Middle High German tigel, tëgel, from Old High German tëgel, tëgal (“earthen vessel”), from Proto-Germanic *digulaz, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Dutch degel (“kettle, boiler, urn”), Danish digel (“crucible”), Swedish degel (“crucible”), Icelandic deigla (“melting pot; crucible”).

With irregular t- (as in tausend) and widespread dialectal -ā- → -ō- from Middle High German dāhen, tāhen, inflected form of dāhe, tāhe, from Old High German thāha, dāha, tāha, from Proto-Germanic *þanhǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to thicken, be solid”), related to *þinhtaz (“dense, tight”).

From Middle High German, from Old High German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þausōną (“to surge, roar, flow”), which is imitative. See also Old English þys (“tempest, storm”), Old Norse þyssa (“uproar, tumult”), Icelandic þysja (“to rush”).

From Middle High German traben, draben, from Old High German *drabōn (“to press; stamp; stomp”), from Proto-Germanic *þrabōną (“to press, drive, compel”). Cognate with Old English þrafian (“to urge, compel; argue”). More at thrave.

parole.significato: a style of clothing or appearance, chiefly one that is typical of some group, region or age; a traditional costume
parole.testo: From Middle High German traht(e), from Old High German trahta, from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz, from the verb *draganą, whence modern tragen, thus originally “that which is borne/worn/carried”. Cognate with Dutch dracht, English draught. Not related to German trachten (“to seek, strive”), although cert

parole.significato: a drink, generally mixed of several ingredients, and often for medical or magical effect; a potion
parole.testo: From Middle High German tranc, from Old High German tranc, from Proto-Germanic *drankiz (“drink; dose; potion”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to pull; draw; sip”); compare Dutch drank (“beverage, drink”), Hunsrik Drank. In its general sense of "something to drink", it was displaced

From Middle High German trūrec, from Old High German trūrag, from Proto-Germanic *dreuzagaz (“bloody”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreus- (“to break, break off, crumble”). By surface analysis, Trauer + -ig. Cognate with Dutch treurig (“sad, gloomy”), Low German trurig (“sad”), Hunsrik traurich (“sad

parole.significato: residue mass from making beer or brandy, draff, marc, pomace
parole.testo: From Middle High German treber, from Old High German trebir, originally a plural of a *trab, from Proto-Germanic *drabaz.

parole.significato: cheat grass; bromegrass; chess (kind of grass growing in fields of corn or grain)
parole.testo: From Middle High German trefs, trefse, later trebse and variants, from Proto-Germanic *drab, *dreb, probably related to *drabaz (“dregs”). As in Wespe (“wasp”), forms with -sp- are found chiefly in northern, Low and Central German, varieties; compare Middle Low German drespe. Related to Dutch dravik

From northern Middle High German trǖge, drǖge, from Proto-Germanic *drūgiz. The form remains dialectally in East Central German treiche and further in Central Franconian drüch, Limburgish druug. Probably cognate with English dry.
From Middle High German triel, from Proto-Germanic *treulaz. Like German trýni (“snout”), derived from an extended form of Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to flay, divide, split”).
Middle High German trollen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *truzlōną (“to lumber”). Perhaps related to trödeln. Cognate of English troll.

parole.significato: steward of a princely household, sewer
parole.testo: From Middle High German truhtsæze (“steward”), from Old High German truhtsāzzo, compound of trucht (“host”) + sazzo (“one who sits”). The first part goes back to Proto-Germanic *druhtiz (“troop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ- (“to support”). Doublet of Drost (“reeve, bailiff”).

parole.significato: A somewhat negative word for a female person, sometimes associated with slovenliness, sometimes more with silliness and…
parole.testo: Perhaps a feminised form of dialectal Upper German Trull, Troll (“coarse, boorish person”), which is probably inherited from Proto-Germanic *truzlą. Cognate with Troll (“troll”), from Old Norse.
From Middle High German trum, drum, from Old High German drum (“splinter, end piece”), from Proto-Germanic *þrumą (“butt, stump”).
From Middle High German trenke, from Old High German trenka, from the root of tränken (“to water, make drink”), from Proto-Germanic *drankijaną.
From Middle High German tugent, from Old High German tugund (“virtue, power”), from Proto-Germanic *dugunþō (“usefulness, virtue”). Cognate with English douth, dought.

parole.significato: to dab (to touch repeatedly with a soft, often moist, object)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tüpfen, tupfen (“to dip, to moisten”), from Old High German tuphen (“to dip, to moisten”), from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną; see *daupijaną (“to dip”). Cognate with English dip. The semantic development is due to association with Middle High German stuphen (“to poke”) and a diale

parole.significato: giant; a troll-like or demonic creature
parole.testo: From Middle High German turse, türse, from Old High German turs, thuris, from Proto-Germanic *þurisaz. Cognate with English thurse, Old Norse þurs.

From Middle High German umbeganc, from Old High German umbigang (“a course, return”), from Proto-Germanic *umbigangaz (“a going around, circuit”), equivalent to um- + Gang (“a gang, going”). Cognate with Dutch omgang, English umgang, Danish omgang, Swedish omgång, Norwegian omgang.
Inherited from Middle High German umstrīten, inherited from Old High German umstrītan, derived from Proto-Germanic *straidijaną (“to fight, to quarrel”).
From Middle High German unbescholten, the negated past participle of Middle High German beschelten, from Old High German biskeltan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skeldaną.
From Middle High German unde, from Old High German unti, from Proto-Germanic *andi, *anþi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti. Compare Dutch en, English and, Danish end.

parole.significato: vermin; pests; restricted to small animals, usually insects or spiders, sometimes also mice, etc.
parole.testo: From early modern German ungeziffer, Ungezieffer, a variant form of Middle High German ungezibere. These pertain to Old High German zebar (“sacrificial animal”) and hence originally meant “animals unsuitable for sacrifice”, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tībrą (“offering, sacrifice, victim”). The w

From Old High German ungilīh, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, un- + gleich. Compare Old English unġelīċ (English unlike), Dutch ongelijk, Old Norse úlíkr (see there for North Germanic descendants).
From Old High German unreht, from Proto-Germanic *unrehtaz. Cognate with English unright, Dutch onrecht.

From Middle High German untāt, from Old High German untāt, from Proto-Germanic *undēdiz. Analysable as un- (“bad, grave”) + Tat (“deed”). Cognate with Middle Dutch ondaet, Middle Low German undāt, Old English undǣd.

parole.significato: severe weather, storm, rainstorm (an instance of weather characterized by strong wind and/or rainfall)
parole.testo: From Middle High German unweter, unwiter, from Old High German unwetar, from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą. By surface analysis, un- (“bad, grave”) + Wetter (“weather”). Cognate with Dutch onweer, English unweather, Swedish oväder, among others.

parole.significato: very, quite, really, total, totally, absolutely
parole.testo: From Middle High German ur-, from Old High German ur-, ir- (“thoroughly”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”).

parole.significato: judgment (the preferred spelling in a legal context), verdict, sentence (court decision)
parole.testo: From Middle High German urteil, from Old High German urteil, urteili, from Proto-Germanic *uzdailiją (“judicial decision; verdict; judgement”). Cognate with Dutch oordeel and English ordeal.
From Middle High German vaterlōs, faterlōs, from Old High German faterlōs, from Proto-Germanic *fadērlausaz, equivalent to Vater + -los. Cognate with English fatherless.

parole.significato: Inseparable verbal prefix indicating privation or the direction of 'forth', 'away'.
parole.testo: From Middle High German ver-, from Old High German far-, fir-, from a mixture of Proto-Germanic *firi- (expresses intensive or perfective meaning), *fra- (“forth, away, off; fully, completely, up”), *furi- (“against, opposed”) and other similar particles. Cognate with English for-, Dutch ver-, Yiddi

ver- + bleuen (“to beat”) or bläuen; from Middle High German bliuwen, from Old High German bliuwan, from Proto-Germanic *blewwaną. Cognates include Dutch blouwen and English blow. Not related to German blau.
From Old High German firbot, from Proto-Germanic *furibudą. Cognate with Dutch verbod, English forbode, Danish forbud, Swedish förbud.
From Middle High German vervarn, from Old High German firfaran, farfaran from Proto-Germanic *frafaraną, equivalent to ver- + fahren.
From Middle High German vergëben, from Old High German fargëban, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną. Analyzable as ver- + geben. Cognate with Dutch vergeven, English forgive, Icelandic fyrirgefa.

parole.significato: to conceal, to hide, to dissemble
parole.testo: From Middle High German verheln, from Old High German firhelan, from Proto-Germanic *frahelaną. By surface analysis, ver- + hehlen.

parole.significato: loss (all senses, except defeat, for which Niederlage is used)
parole.testo: From Middle High German verlust, from Old High German farlust, from Proto-Germanic *fralustiz. Ultimately related to verlieren.
From Proto-Germanic *maþlijaną.

From Middle High German verruochet, participle of Middle High German verruochen (“to stop caring about something”), compound of ruochen (“to care”), from Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną (“to care, take care”). Related to geruhen (“to deign, condescend”) and ruchlos (“reckless”).

From Middle High German verstān, virstēn, vorstēn, ferstān, from Old High German firstān, firstēn, from Proto-Germanic *frastāną, equivalent to ver- + stehen. Cognate with Bavarian versteh, Dutch verstaan, Middle Low German vorstān. Compare also English forstand.
From Middle High German vertragen, from Old High German firtragan, fartragan, from Proto-Germanic *fradraganą, equal to ver- + tragen. Cognate with Middle Low German verdragen, Dutch verdragen.

parole.significato: to turn, to change, to transform
parole.testo: From Middle High German verwandelen, ferwandelen, from Old High German firwantalōn, from Proto-Germanic *frawandlōną, equivalent to ver- + wandeln. Cognate with Low German verwanneln, Saterland Frisian ferwondelje.
ver- + wittern, from Middle High German witeren, from Middle High German weter, from Old High German wetar. From Proto-Germanic *wedrą (“weather”), eventually from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰrom.

parole.significato: to get caught up in the minutiae of, or pursue an inexpedient approach to, a task, problem, or affair
parole.testo: Frequentative of Middle High German verzetten (“to scatter, disperse”), from ver- + Old High German zetten (“to spread”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tadjaną (“to strew, scatter”). Combination of zetten with the instrumental suffix -eln yielded the cognate noun Zettel (“warp”); its etymologicall

parole.significato: animal, beast, any kind but especially an insect or pest
parole.testo: Doublet of Vieh from Upper German. Hence from Middle High German vihe, from Old High German fihu, from Proto-Germanic *fehu, from Proto-Indo-European *peḱu- (“livestock, domestic animals”).

From Middle High German vierzehen, from Old High German fiorzehan, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun. Equivalent to vier + zehn. Compare Dutch veertien, West Frisian fjirtjin, English fourteen, Danish fjorten, Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌳𐍅𐍉𐍂𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌿𐌽 (fidwōrtaihun).
From Middle High German vierzic, from Old High German fiorzug, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr tigiwiz, equivalent to vier + -zig.

From Middle High German von(e) (“from”), from Old High German fon(a), alongside rarer northern fan(a). It is uncertain whether the High German o-vocalism continues an original Proto-Germanic *funē, comparable with Sanskrit पुनः- (punaḥ-), or whether it is an atonic alteration of Proto-West Germanic

From Middle High German vormunde, from Old High German foramunto, a compound of fora (“before, in front of”, whence German vor) + munt (“hand; protection; guardianship”), the latter from Proto-Germanic *mundō. In contemporary understanding it is usually reanalysed as vor + Mund (“mouth”, unrelated w

In the sense “omen” from Middle High German vorzeichen, from Old High German forazeihhan, from Proto-Germanic *furaitaikną. Cognate with Old English foretācen (English foretoken). In the technical senses simply from vor- (“before, in front”) + Zeichen (“sign”).
From Middle High German veterlich, vaterlich, from Old High German faterlīh, from Proto-Germanic *fadurlīkaz, equivalent to Vater + -lich. Cognate with English fatherly, Dutch vaderlijk.

From Middle High German vogelen, vogeln, from Old High German fogalōn (“catch birds”). Related to Vogel (“bird”), from Proto-Germanic *fuglaz (“bird”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleu (“to flow, to float”). Cognate with English fowl.
From Middle High German wahs, from Old High German wahs, from Proto-Germanic *wahsą. Akin to Luxembourgish Wuess, Dutch was, English wax, Danish voks, Swedish vax.
From Middle High German wahstuom, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wahstmaz (“growth”). By surface analysis, wachsen + -tum. Cognate with Old English wæstm (“growth, increase, produce, fruit”).
From Middle High German wade, from Old High German wado, from Proto-Germanic *waþwô (“curve; muscle; calf of the leg”), from Proto-Indo-European *wat- (“curved”).

Coined in the 15th century after the model of wahnwitzig which uses as its first part the word wahn, which came from Old High German wan "missing, empty", which came from Proto-Germanic *wanaz. Not cognate with Wahn. Cognate with English wane.

parole.significato: a bevelled roof, particularly if triangular and in a gable
parole.testo: From Middle High German walbe, from Old High German walbo (“vault; vaulted roof”), from Proto-Germanic *hwalbô. Related to Old Norse hvalf, Old English hwealf. See whelm.

From Middle High German walstat, from wal (“battlefield”, originally probably “battle, carnage”) + stat (“place”, whence modern Stadt, Statt, and Stätte). The first element is from Old High German wal, from Proto-Germanic *walaz.
From Middle High German, from Old High German walzan (“to turn”), from Proto-Germanic *waltaną (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn”).

From Middle High German want, from Old High German want, from Proto-Germanic *wanduz (“fence, wall”), from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn; bend; wind; twist; braid; weave”). Cognate with English wand although developing a completely distinct meaning.
From Middle High German warze, Old High German warza, from Proto-Germanic *wartǭ. Cognate with Old Norse varta, Old English wearte, Dutch wrat (“to grow”), English wart, Gothic *𐍅𐌰𐍂𐍄𐍉 (*wartō).
From Middle High German waten, from Old High German watan, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną. The form is East Central German with open-syllable lengthening before -t-; compare the variants above.

From Middle High German wëhseln, from Old High German *wëhsalōn, from Proto-Germanic *wihslōną, from Proto-Indo-European *weyk-, *weyḱ- (“to change”). Compare Dutch wisselen, Luxembourgish wiesselen, dialectal English wissle, more distantly Latin vicis, English week, German Woche.
From Middle High German wecke, from Old High German wecki, weggi (“wedge”), from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz. Cognate with Dutch wig (“wedge”), English wedge.

From Middle High German wecke, from Old High German wecki, weggi (“wedge; wedge-shaped baked good”), from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz (“wedge”). Cognate with Dutch wig (“wedge”), English wedge; also Lithuanian vãgis (“hook, peg”).
From the compounding of the prefix weg (“away”) and fliegen (“to fly”), from Old High German fliogan (“to fly”), from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”).
From Middle High German wēwe, from Old High German wēwo, from Proto-Germanic *waiwô.
From Middle High German wīplich, from Old High German wīblīh, from Proto-Germanic *wībalīkaz, equivalent to Weib + -lich. Cognate with Dutch wijfelijk, English wifely.

parole.significato: sour cherry (fruit of the sour cherry tree)
parole.testo: From Middle High German wīhsel, from Old High German wīhsila, from Proto-Germanic *wīhsilō.

From Middle High German wīde, from Old High German wīda, from Proto-Germanic *wīþijō (“willow”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis (“that which twines or bends, branch, switch”). Cognate to Dutch wijde (“willow”), Swedish vide, English withy.
From Old High German wīo, from Proto-Germanic *wīwô. Compare Pennsylvania German Woi.

From Middle High German weinen, from Old High German weinōn (“to cry, lament, cry woe”), from Proto-Germanic *wainōną (“to cry, weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *wáy (“woe”). Related with Weh, English woe, which see. Cognate with Dutch wenen (“to weep, to cry”), Old English wānian (“to complain, lam
Equivalent to Wein (“wine”) + Fass (“keg”); from Middle High German wīnvaz, from Old High German wīnfaz, from Proto-Germanic *wīnafatą. Cognate with Icelandic vínfat.
From Old High German wīsa, from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“wise”).
From Middle High German wīse, from Old High German wīsi (a variant of wīs), from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz. Cognate with Dutch wijs, English wise.
From Middle High German wīt, from Old High German wīt, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz. Compare Low German wied, Hunsrik weid, Dutch wijd, English wide, Danish vid.
From Middle High German welch, wilich, from Old High German welih, wilih, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz.
From Middle High German welich, from Old High German welih, wilih, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz. Compare English which.
